articles.title: Denmark ratifies security deal with US and Greenland
articles.summary: The deal provides the US with expanded military access, on top of what it already had based on a previous agreement. It comes after threats by US President Trump to take Greenland with force.

image.caption: Greenland is an autonomous Arctic island under Danish controlImage: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Denmark'sparliament on Thursday ratified a security agreement with the USover Greenland, hoping to end tensions after US President Donald Trump had repeatedly demanded control over the autonomous Danish territory.
In the Danish 179-seat parliament, all 109 members present voted in favor of the text. Greenland's parliament already ratified the deal in early November.

US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the ratification, saying in a post on X: "The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO."
What does the Danish-US security agreement over Greenland include?

The trilateral security and military access agreement between Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen allows for expanded US military presence on the mineral-rich and strategically located island in the northern Atlantic.
It also includes permission to establish a "Golden ‌Dome" ​missile defense system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
The island is home to some 57,000 people and is strategically located along the shortest route from Europe to North America. It already is home to the northernmost US military base.

The deal was signed in September by Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen but still needed ratification from lawmakers in Greenland and Denmark.

blocks.caption: Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen signed the deal in SeptemberImage: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Trump's threats to take Greenland by force
In January 2026, Trump renewed calls for Greenland to become part of the US, threatening military action and tariffs against European allies if they opposed him.
He argued that Denmark was not able to protect the autonomous Arctic territory from threats by China and Russia. His demands strained US relations with Denmark and alarmed European NATO allies.

Tensions somewhat eased in late January when Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte announced a "concept of a deal" that would expand US military access to Greenland. This then led to the agreement being signed in September.

Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has broad military access to Greenland. Denmark had repeatedly said it was open to expanding the US military presence on the island but rejected Trump's demand for full US control.

articles.title: New law ‘may be needed’ after Google rejects call to remove Russell Brand’s YouTube prison message
articles.summary: Ex-minister Jess Phillips admits government does not have power to compel platforms to remove distressing content

blocks.text: A new online safety act is likely to be needed to tackle convicted criminals such as Russell Brand using social media platforms to broadcast messages from prison, Labour MP Jess Phillips has said.

Just days after his conviction, Brand’s wife, Laura, broadcast a message from her husband to their 6.6 million YouTube subscribers, claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences for which he had been convicted by a jury. The video has had almost 850,000 views.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) launched an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules. Google, which owns YouTube, has rejected a UK government request, made via the Prison Service, for the video to be taken down amid warnings that it was causing distress to sexual abuse survivors.

A Google spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”

blocks.caption: Laura Brand read out a message from her imprisoned husband on the couple’s YouTube channel on Sunday.  Photograph: Russell Brand/Youtube

blocks.text: Phillips, a former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, admitted the government did not have the power to compel platforms to remove distressing content of this kind.
“Ofcom codes on women’s safety online are just voluntary and frankly voluntary codes to tech companies is the triumph of hope over experience,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
“This is an entirely new era and frankly the regulations are almost certainly not in place for the government to just demand that this be taken down.”

Passed in 2023, the Online Safety Act works to protect social media users from illegal content, as well as ensuring under-18s are not exposed to content that is not age-appropriate, such as pornography. It is being introduced on a phased basis and was expanded this year by additional legislation, updating Ofcom codes of practice. It does not explicitly address the issue of prisoners using social media platforms to directly communicate with the outside world, which in light of Brand’s platform, Phillips accepts is not sufficient.
“Regulatory frameworks, changes and potentially a second online safety act is needed, because before we haven’t had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings,” she said.
Phillips said that pressure would continue to build on organisations such as Google.
“All Google do by leaving this up is show that those codes are not good enough,” she added.

“I think it [a new online safety act] is very likely and the more that these companies show that they are not putting victims at the absolute heart of their policymaking in their content within their own content schemes. If Google want less regulation they will take this down.”
Calls by voices including the victims’ commissioner for London, Andrea Simon, for action to be taken by Google were joined on Thursday morning by ministers.
after newsletter promotion

“I hope they make the same decision that Meta has,” said the minister for children and families, Josh MacAlister, noting that the parent company of Facebook had disabled Brand’s social media accounts on the basis they breached standards prohibiting accounts that were “harmful to the community”.
Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, told Sky News: “It’s quite a disturbing video, actually, but abhorrent in the message it’s conveying.”

“Imagine if you’re one of the victims of Brand’s heinous crimes and you see that video. Prisoners are already banned from making statements to the media. We think this is an exceptional case where MoJ ministers have asked Google to remove this specific content and we hope they’ll do so.”

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said she was concerned if prisoners were able to use conduits in prison to send messages, but felt that Brand’s wife was a separate person and YouTube was “a private platform”.
“Immediately demanding that private platforms take down without looking at whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from,” she said.

While the Brand case has brought the issue into sharp focus, there has been concern in the past about the continued ability to retain a presence on social media of other figures such as Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson.

Filipiñana film still

MANILA, Philippines – Jorrybell Agoto, the lead actress of Filipiñana, passed away, Epicmedia Productions announced on Thursday, November 19.

Agoto’s death comes just a day after the people behind “Jorrybell Beats It” held an acoustic night on Wednesday, November 18 to help raise funds for her hospitalization and medical expenses.
Details of Agoto’s memorial services have yet to be announced.

Filipiñana is the Philippines’ official entry to the 2027 Oscars under the Best International Feature Film category. The shortlists will be announced on December 16, while the awards ceremony will be held on March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, Los Angeles. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Rappler Investigates] Conflict of interest
articles.summary: Like a plague, this affliction has spread across both local and national offices, facilitated by the prevalence of political dynasties

blocks.text: It’s been a recurring theme in several stories we’ve published lately. It’s widespread, taken for granted, and its violation quite brazen among some government officials.

A conflict of interest occurs when private interests threaten to cloud or sway judgment. Public officials are discouraged from placing themselves in such a position because the temptation to exploit contracts, policies, and rulings for personal gain becomes harder to resist.
Ethics and moral principles also dictate that public officials and employees not extend favors or benefits to their relatives.
One would think the rationale is obvious: without it, government looks less like public service and more like a machine for dispensing, if not harvesting, favors.

One of our Aries Rufo Journalism fellows for 2026, Euni Barreno, with the guidance of senior editor Mia Gonzalez, reported on how public works deals involving in-laws of Caloocan City Mayor Along Malapitan raise conflict-of-interest questions.
Euni is a young, graduating journalism student at the University of the Philippines in Diliman and is a news staffer of the Philippine Collegian.
Instead of being inspired by local officials, an aspiring journalist who must report on the apparent misjudgments, if not misdeeds, of his own mayor may end up disheartened.

In his digging, Euni discovered that the recipient of multiple Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) contracts in Caloocan City, a firm named Ave-Mira Construction and Trading, is run by the in-laws of Mayor Along Malapitan.
From 2019 to 2025, according to Euni, Ave-Mira bagged 39 DPWH projects in Caloocan City worth over P731 million. During this period, Along’s father Oscar was an elected official of the city.
The Malapitans have held the mayoral post for more than a decade, with father and son taking turns after being term-limited.

Did laws on conflict of interest deter Along Malapitan and his in-laws from forging DPWH deals in Caloocan City? Apparently not. But they are not alone, unfortunately. A quick scan of recent stories yielded the following:

items: Sara Duterte’s company won millions’ worth of contracts from Davao City Hall (2026)
DOH undersecretary’s brother lands P141 million in health infrastructure projects (2026)
TRACKER: Public officials with links to government contractors (2025)
Lawmakers and construction firm contractors: The ties that bind (2025)
Beyond flood control: DPWH contracts linked to public officials since 2016 (2025)
Bulacan vice mayor’s firm bags P3.5-B DPWH contracts mostly in his hometown (2025)

blocks.text: Like a plague, this affliction has spread across both local and national offices, facilitated by the prevalence of political dynasties.

Yet we are far from being deficient in laws and principles that prohibit these and frown upon conflict of interest in government. There’s the Constitution, Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards, Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and even the Local Government Code. Too many laws but very poor enforcement.
No wonder they are regarded as mere suggestions rather than strictures for compliance. Besides, who has been fined or jailed for violating conflict of interest laws?

A profile by justice reporter Jairo Bolledo of newly-appointed Supreme Court Associate Justice Gamaliel Cordoba reminded me of the new magistrate’s ties to a commercial fishing company, Mercidar Fishing Corporation. It’s partly owned by his wife.

Was it coincidence that when Cordoba was still with the National Telecommunications Commission, the agency stopped issuing service numbers for trackers attached to fishing vessels? These trackers were intended to prevent illegal fishing within 15 kilometers of municipal waters because these are reserved exclusively for small fisherfolk.

It’s little protection for fishing boats that can’t compete with larger commercial vessels. But in 2023, a Malabon regional trial court allowed Mercidar to fish within the 15-kilometer zone. This was affirmed a year later by the High Court — of which Cordoba is now part.
What did I say about conflict of interest again? Till Thursday after next!

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 5:57pm
Gamaliel Cordoba took his oath on Thursday as the new Supreme Court (SC) Associate Justice, succeeding Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, who retired on November 16, 2026.
He took his oath before Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda at the High Court's Session Hall.
Prior to his appointment, Cordoba served as the chairperson of the Commission on Audit (COA), having been appointed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on October 21, 2022.
During his time at COA, the agency submitted at least 50 fraud audit reports to the Office of the Ombudsman and the Independent Commission for Infrastructure.
He also institutionalized GPS-based geotagging of all government infrastructure projects nationwide to ensure proper verification of project status.

Upon the announcement of Cordoba's appointment, Malacañang said that reassigning a leader to a different agency does not signify a loss of the President's trust; instead he sees their potential to do even better in the new role.

"Nakikita ng Pangulo sino yung mga taong nararapat na makasama at manatili sa administrasyon. Nakikita niya kung ano yung kanilang mga potensyal. Nakitaan niya ng kagalingan so ilalagay niya sa mga pwesto na mas kakailanganin pa ang kanilang galing," Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a press briefing.
(The President knows who is deserving to join and stay in the administration. He sees their potential. If he sees their potential, he will place them in agencies where they show their abilities.)
Cordoba also served the longest term as commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC), serving under four administrations from 2009-2022.
From 2008 to 2009, Cordoba also served on the Board of Directors of the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR).
He also held several key positions under the Arroyo administration at the Office of the President.
Cordoba obtained his Bachelor of Arts in Economics in 1992 and Juris Doctor in 1996 at the Ateneo de Manila University. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Comelec reminds public: No fees for voter certifications
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Thursday reminded the public that voter certifications are issued free of charge nationwide amid reports of social media posts falsely…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Thursday reminded the public that voter certifications are issued free of charge nationwide amid reports of social media posts falsely claiming that applicants were being charged for the document.
Comelec Chair George Erwin Garcia said the certification is free regardless of the number of copies requested or whether it is obtained from the commission’s main office or any of its field offices.
“Comelec gives all voter certifications for free in the whole Philippines, whether it is here in the main office or in the field, there is no fee,” Garcia said.

He cited reports circulating in Sultan Kudarat province alleging that applicants were being asked to pay P20 for each voter certification. However, Garcia said the commission’s verification found that the post came from a fake account.
“We verified, we counter-checked; it turns out that it is a fake account. So there are people like that,” he said.
The Comelec had earlier reiterated that voter certifications have been issued free of charge since 2022 as part of its efforts to “streamline frontline registration services.”
Separately, the Comelec Region XII office also addressed a social media post alleging that a voter was charged P20 for a certification at the Comelec office in Matalam, North Cotabato.
In a statement posted on social media, the regional office stressed that voter certifications are free and warned against unauthorized fee collection.
“We wish to emphasize that the issuance of Voter Certification is FREE OF CHARGE under existing COMELEC rules. We will not tolerate any unauthorized collection of fees,” it said.
The regional office said it had launched an investigation and was reaching out to the owner of the social media account to obtain her account of the incident and any available evidence.
It also denied an allegation that its office had referred to the complainant as “reklamador.”
“For the record, no such communication has been made by our Office, nor has any such remark been uttered by us,” it said.
The regional office said it was taking the matter seriously and remained committed to upholding accountability, professionalism and integrity in its services.
“The public deserves honest, fair, and free electoral services,” it said. /jpv

articles.title: Trump, Xi, Putin begin historic meeting with Ukraine war on agenda
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin began an unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday, where they said they will discuss the war in…

image.caption: President Donald Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for their trilateral meeting, at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Doug Mills/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin began an unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday, where they said they will discuss the war in Ukraine and nuclear arms control.
The trilateral is unlikely to produce major agreements, analysts say

Sat around a big round table in a villa in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit, the leaders of ‌the world's biggest nuclear powers took turns to give opening remarks.
"We are really making history," Trump said. "The three of us have a great deal to discuss.”
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin said the three countries have "numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine.”

items: Xi, Putin and Trump expected to meet for about an hour, Kremlin says

blocks.text: Unlike Trump and Putin, Xi — who Chinese state media said was presiding over the meeting — did not make a reference to Ukraine, but said: "History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers ​clash, the world falls into turmoil."

The trilateral is unlikely to produce major agreements, analysts say, given deep differences over ​Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. But it has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.
Before the meeting, Trump met Xi and Putin separately, referring to both as friends.

Trump said both he and Xi felt strongly about oil having to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been disrupted by the Iran war. ​Xi has not mentioned Ukraine or Iran in any of his remarks during the two-day summit so far.

Patricia Kim, foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution, said ⁠China would not want to be seen as ⁠brokering a deal over Ukraine, given the "problematic optics" of Kyiv and European leaders not taking part.
"Xi has characterized the ‌Russia-Ukraine war as fundamentally a European problem, making Beijing even less inclined to assume responsibility for resolving it," Kim said.
Fanfare and pageantry

Speaking to Fox News earlier, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival for the summit, which contrasted with the more muted greeting of other leaders, including Putin. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony.
Japan's relations with China have soured since Takaichi's remarks in 2025, when she said Japan could deploy its military if a Chinese move on Taiwan also threatened its territory.
Takaichi, who cut an isolated figure throughout the ⁠summit, said Tokyo's position on Taiwan had not changedsince 1972.

items: How China is positioning itself as a global leader as it hosts Trump, Putin

blocks.text: Japan and Taiwan this week reported Russian military aircraft incursions as Moscow displayed it can still project power in Asia despite being busy in Ukraine. On Taiwan, Xi told Trump the U.S. must "do the right thing" to avoid major setbacks in their relationship.

Xi greeted Trump at the airport, the first time he has done so with any visiting leader since becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart's gesture at Joint ‌Base Andrews in September when they last met. The leaders also briefly hugged.
"This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he's never gone to the airport to meet somebody," Trump said.

"And not only that, the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing. It was great respect, and I appreciate that. That's a big win for us. It's a big win for China too."
Trump, Xi and Putin set for historic top nuclear powers meeting
Trump arrived after Xi and Putin delivered pointed speeches denouncing Western trade "protectionism" and sanctions.

During Thursday's APEC proceedings, Xi ​called for "free and open" trade. Western leaders say China's growth model favoring industrial strength over consumers is unfair and creates destabilizing global trade imbalances.
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said Russia was key for ⁠food and energy security in the Asia-Pacific.
Trump, reeling from a mid-term election loss and the Nvidia spy scandal, told the audience the U.S. has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years.
Tough nuclear arms discussion
Trump has insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit, despite China's repeated objections to joining talks with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.
“It’s not an easy thing ⁠to do - give ⁠them up,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of their meeting.

The ​leaders have plenty of reasons to appear together but far fewer to agree on substance, given differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons, trade and China's military buildup, said Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defense of ​Democracies.
"A photograph could serve all three men well," Singleton said, adding ⁠that he thought the "agenda is much harder to agree on."

Trump's talks with Xi come after an extension of their trade truce this month, but also amid growing tension over reports of Nvidia chips being diverted to China through Southeast Asia, raising questions about the effectiveness of U.S. export curbs and the future of Chinese access to advanced technology.
"This is Beijing's worst nightmare. China wants chip access that it can negotiate with the president. It may get chip restrictions written into law by both parties," Singleton said.

articles.title: Cocaine smuggler avoids prison sentence, as judge seeks to keep child out of foster care
articles.summary: A man who played a pivotal role in smuggling more than three kilograms of cocaine into Newfoundland has staved off a federal prison sentence, as a judge sought to keep the man's son from going into…

image.caption: An Ontario judge has sentenced a convicted drug smuggler to house arrest to avoid his son going into foster care. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

A man who played a pivotal role in smuggling more than three kilograms of cocaine into Newfoundland has staved off a federal prison sentence, as a judge sought to keep the man's son from going into foster care.
Justice Louis Strezos hopes sentence can help avoid intergenerational cycle
Steven Armstrong will spend two years less a day on house arrest, to be followed by three years of probation, in what Justice Louis Strezos admitted was an "extraordinary result."

Armstrong has become a single father in the years since his arrest for drug trafficking in 2020. The court heard his son has exceptional needs, and Armstrong is the only person capable of caring for him.
"This is a difficult sentencing decision," reads the first line of the judge's ruling.

The Crown had initially been seeking a sentence of up to seven years in prison, arguing Armstrong was not eligible for house arrest due to the nature of the offence and a lengthy criminal record for drug-related offences.
Prosecutor Christopher Kalantzis lowered his recommendation to four-to-five years after Armstrong's two co-accused were sentenced in Newfoundland and Labrador.

items: Court case shows how cocaine traffickers got creative during N.L.'s COVID-19 restrictions

blocks.text: Dion Wilson Lee Rodgers was given a 39-month penitentiary term, while Edmond Dorman Pickett received 34 months.
Strezos agreed with Kalantzis that on the surface of the case, Armstrong should not be eligible for a conditional sentence order — more commonly referred to as house arrest.
"Ordinarily, he would be correct," the judge wrote.
Caring for boy is rehabilitative, judge says

However, Strezos accepted arguments from Armstrong's lawyer, Adam Boni, about how a prison sentence would be destructive to Armstrong's son, and put him in the same child welfare system that played a significant role in his father's criminality.

Steven Armstrong grew up without a father. His mother died by suicide when he was young. He was raised in group homes, where he became addicted to drugs. His criminal record started as a youth and continued up to 2011, when he was given a three-year prison sentence for drug trafficking.

items: Cocaine smuggler could avoid prison as judge fears incarceration would orphan man's son

blocks.text: Strezos also accepted Boni's argument that caring for his son has had a significant impact on Armstrong's life, kickstarting the process of rehabilitation long before a sentence was imposed.

"[The boy] has contributed to ending the cycle of the offender's criminality. Mr. Armstrong has been and will continue to be rehabilitated by caring for [him] — the 'twist of fate' aptly described by Mr. Boni," Strezos wrote.
The judge also considered letters of support, including ones from Armstrong's aunt and the boy's doctor.

"If Steven were to go to jail, it would be very detrimental to [his son] in my opinion," wrote Joan Armstrong. "Steven and [his son] are joined at the hip. I worry that the emotional toll on [him] would cause him serious harm, and cause him to regress."

"I would strongly support the possibility of house arrest rather than Steven being away from parenting time with [his son] over these important years of [his] development," the unnamed pediatrician wrote.
RCMP takedown a year in the making
Police had been watching Armstrong for more than a year before his arrest in September of 2020.

Court records show the investigation began as a probe into a central Newfoundland man and his criminal associates in 2019. During the investigation, police noticed Armstrong had made multiple short trips to the island.

Armstrong was stopped during one of those visits in 2019, but police failed to find any drugs in his vehicle. Investigators continued tracking Armstrong into 2020, when they learned he planned to transport a pickup truck to Newfoundland. The province went into lockdown in March due to the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving Armstrong unable to gain entry.

In September 2020, police followed Armstrong as he left Ontario in a 2006 Honda Ridgeline. He left the truck in a Canadian Tire parking lot in North Sydney, N.S., where Rodgers and his stepfather picked it up and drove it back to Newfoundland.
Police found 3.4 kilograms of cocaine hidden inside the truck's passenger side airbag compartment.
Judge gives warning to Armstrong
Strezos concluded a total of five years supervision — two on house arrest and three on probation — is proportionate given the "unique circumstances of this case."
The sentence will include GPS monitoring, close geographic confinement when Armstrong is not at home, some tailored exceptions and reporting to Strezos every six months.
Armstrong must also submit a DNA sample and is prohibited from owning weapons for the rest of his life.
The judge's ruling ended with a warning.
"Mr. Armstrong, I assure you that if you breach any term of this sentence, you will go to prison."

articles.title: South Korea's top court overturns jail term for former PM Han
articles.summary: Former Prime Minister Han Duck-so was convicted of helping legitimize the 2024 martial law declaration. The case will now return to a lower court.

image.caption: Han was convicted after helping to make the ex-President Yoon's martial law bid seem more legitimateImage: Kim Do-hoon/Yonhap/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The South Korean Supreme Court on Thursday overturned a 15-year prison sentence for the country's former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for playing a key role in the 2024 imposition of martial law by ex-President Yoon Suk Yeol.
The case will now return to a lower court, the Seoul High Court, which had sentenced Han to 15 years in prison in May.
Why was South Korean ex-PM Han's sentence overturned?
Han was convicted for helping plan the insurrection by suggesting that Yoon hold a Cabinet meeting to make martial law seem legitimate.
He also allegedly tried to collect Cabinet members' signatures on a related document and reviewed orders to cut off power and water to media outlets critical of Yoon.
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that prosecutors had not sufficiently proven the case and ordered a review of the conviction.
At the same time, the top court upheld a four-year prison term for Yoon's wife, Kim Keon Hee, on charges of corruption, including manipulating stock prices and bribery.
South Korea's Yoon Suk Yeol sentenced to life in prison
What was the 2024 insurrection?
On December 3, 2024, former president Yoon Suk Yeol abruptly declared martial law, prompting massive protests and a showdown in parliament.
At the time, Yoon said the declaration was needed to rid the country of "pro-North Korean forces" and followed it by sending troops and police into parliament.
But enough lawmakers managed to enter the assembly chamber to unanimously vote down Yoon's decree, forcing his cabinet to rescind it.
Yoon was impeached and later found guitly of leading an insurrection and sentenced to life in prison.

articles.title: Badenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’ – UK politics live
articles.summary:
PM has asked Badenoch to withdraw her suggestion that benefits should be cut because ‘double amputees run marathons’

Alexandra Topping is a Guardian political…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 8m agoBadenoch says it's 'disturbing' that Xi, Trump and Putin look like they're 'trying to carve up world between them'
23m agoBadenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’

blocks.text: Badenoch says it's 'disturbing' that Xi, Trump and Putin look like they're 'trying to carve up world between them'

blocks.caption: Alexandra Topping

blocks.text: Alexandra Topping
Alexandra Topping is a Guardian political correspondent.

Kemi Badenoch was in a straight-talking mode on the media round this morning, calling the historic meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin “disturbing”, saying it looked like they were trying to “carve” up the world” between them.
Speaking on the Today programme, the leader of the opposition said the meeting was “absolutely not reassuring”.
She said:

double quotation markThere are three world leaders who look like they’re trying to carve up the world between them, a tri-polar world where Xi gets Asia, America gets the western hemisphere and Russia gets Europe, and that is very concerning, especially seeing Donald Trump call President Putin his friend. Russia is not America’s friend, it certainly hasn’t been during my lifetime. But also at a time when we’re all worried about where the Ukraine war is going, the message that is sending to President Zelensky and of course the other summit that is taking place … is very concerning indeed. And what I want to know is where we fit in in all of this. I don’t want to be in a polarised world run by Russia. I’ll do everything I can to make sure that doesn’t happen.

Badenoch went further than the prime minister, who was asked about the meeting by Ed Davey at prime minister’s questions yesterday. The Liberal Democrat leader said “the security implications of Trump, Putin and Xi cosying up” should highlight the need for a fresh deal with the European Union.

Burnham replied that he would be in Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing to support Ukraine in China, but stopped short of expressing concern about the meeting of the three world leaders.
He said:

double quotation markThe thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine and that is what this government will do. And on this issue, I do pay tribute to all sides of the house because that is what we’ve managed to do in the years since the conflict began and that is the right thing to do … Let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in [China] – this country is squarely with Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Ed Davey at PMQs yesterday. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: Badenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’

Good morning. At PMQs yesterday Andy Burnham said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw the “double amputees run marathons” comment that she used to justify the Tory plan to cut sickness and disability benefits by £14bn. It was “crass and insensitive”, he said.
This morning Badenoch defended what she was saying claimed that, in fact, she was delivering a “message of hope”.
In an interview on the Today programme, asked if she accepted that her remark was insensitive, Badenoch said she didn’t. She went on:

double quotation markI will speak the truth and I will say what I believe is common sense. And what I know is that, if people can work, then we should encourage them to work. And what I’m saying is actually a message of hope, that if people even with significant, problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work.

When the presenter, Nick Robinson, put it to her that it was unreasonable to use an exceptional case as a guide to what most disabled people should be doing, Badenoch did not agree. “We do use extreme examples to illustrate things,” she said.

Robinson tried again, saying she was taking “one extreme case [to] imply that anybody on disability benefits should just get on with it”. Badenoch accused him of “faux outrage” and “tone policing”. She added:
double quotation markPeople are free to disagree, but they know where I’m coming from. I will post more from the interview shortly.
Today the news will be dominated by two summits. This afternoon Burnham is in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. We have coverage of this on our Europe live blog.
And in China, Vladimir Putin, who invaded Ukraine, Xi Jinping, his leading ally, and Donald Trump, who is seen by many as a closet Putin ally, are meeting now. You can read about that here.

We will have comments open in about an hour. That is because I will be doing a Q&A this afternoon, probably from about 3pm, and I will try to answer as many questions as possible. Do post them below the line.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister, takes questions in the Commons.

10am: The Conservative party announces the results of the first round of voting in the election of its candidate for London mayor for 2028. James Cleverly, the former home secretary and former foreign secretary, is expected to get more than 50% of the vote, meaning a second round of voting should not be necessary.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
Noon: Heather Hallett, the Covid inquiry chair, publishes her report on the test, trace and isolate system.

Around 12.15pm (UK time): Andy Burnham arrives in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. He is expected to speak to the media later in the afternoon after the plenary has finished.
1pm: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, attends a meeting of the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference in Dublin.

articles.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
articles.summary: Survivors reject relocation plans they say ignore their safety, land rights and livelihoods

blocks.text: ByOndiro Oganga and Swaibu IbrahimBBC AfricaReporting fromKampala
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
The landslide struck Bududa in 2019, killing more than 53 people, including 33 children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family members.
"My quest should be a lesson," he said.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18 million Ugandan shillings ($4,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.

Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8 million shillings ($1,900), plus 10 million shillings (about $2,400) towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.

The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.

"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.

The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.

"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.
"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.
The complainants say relocation must involve more than move people out of danger.
They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.
The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

articles.title: BAE to slash 1,000 jobs across head office and air business to streamline orders
articles.summary:
Job cuts to exclude shop floor, aircraft maintenance and trainees but move prompts calls for more orders to support British defence giant

BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than…

blocks.text: BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor.

The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”.

The cuts represent about 2% of its 50,000 strong workforce in the UK, which includes about 18,500 in its air business and about 1,000 in its head office in London. They will be made through voluntary redundancies and will exclude people working on the shop floor, aircraft maintenance at RAF bases and early career trainees.

A spokesperson for BAE said the cuts represented the “next stage of our ongoing focus on enhancing our agility and competitiveness, so we can help to maximise the value of every pound our customers spend on defence.
“We recognise that this news may be unsettling for our people and we’re focused on achieving potential workforce reductions through a voluntary process,” they said.

BAE last year received an order for 20 Typhoon fighter jets from Turkey, in a deal announced at the factory by Keir Starmer. However, that order is thought to provide only two years of work at the Lancashire factories – not enough to sustain jobs until production starts on the next generation of fighters. BAE will lead production of the sixth-generation Tempest fighter in an alliance with Italy and Japan.
A source with knowledge of the matter said that the job cuts were linked to uncertainty over the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet programme, more than cost-cutting.

The move comes even as BAE has benefited from a boom in defence spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, the company told its investors it had secured £33bn in orders so far this year and that it expected further contracts before the end of 2026. It also raised its free cashflow guidance for its financial year by 10%, from about £2bn to £3bn.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the union Unite, warned that there would not be a manufacturing industry left in the UK “if the government doesn’t start making critical decisions”.
“To stop the erosion of defence jobs and get the growth we need, the government needs to announce contracts for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) immediately,” she said.
BAE unveiled the uncrewed CCA – which is named Brontanax – at the Farnborough International airshow in July.
Andrew Snowden, a Conservative MP in Lancashire where BAE has two air manufacturing hubs, echoed Graham’s call for more government support.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: BAE Systems reveals Brontanax unmanned fighter aircraft at Farnborough International Airshow in Hampshire in July 2026.  Photograph: Sarah Young/Reuters

blocks.text: He told the Lancashire Post: “The government should act now to support BAE by placing orders for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, giving skilled workers and the supply chain here in Lancashire a clear pipeline of work.”

It comes with the government also under pressure to reach a decision on its Skynet military satellite replacement. American weapons maker Lockheed Martin was thought to be the Ministry of Defence’s preferred choice, but ministers have delayed the choice after Unite argued it would lead to UK job cuts at rival Airbus’s existing factories.
An MoD spokesperson said: “We know that any potential voluntary redundancies can cause concerns and our thoughts are with those potentially affected.
“This government is delivering the biggest boost in defence spending since the cold ar, having already agreed £4bn worth of investments since July.

“This includes awarding BAE a £708m contract extension to lead the Global Combat Air Programme developments and supporting the £8bn contract to supply Turkey with 20 Typhoon jets last year, which sustains 6,000 jobs at two BAE sites.”

articles.title: Is ‘interoperability’ the future of marketing?
articles.summary: At DigiCon 2026, marketing trailblazers define the word through lived experiences

items: The concept of 'interoperability' is introduced as a more structured form of collaboration, emphasizing cross-industry partnerships and the integration of technology and human creativity.
The event showcased how interoperability fosters community building and collaboration in pop culture, illustrating its potential to inspire collective action and creativity in the face of challenges.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Digital Marketing Association of the Philippines (DMAP) and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

The word “collaboration” has been frequently thrown around in the past years – rising influencers joining forces with brands on a series of social media postings, vloggers coming together on their individual channels, and online creators of entirely different disciplines linking for passion projects to fill in each other’s “gaps” or introduce new areas for exploration for each other’s audiences.

While it’s cool to witness these many forms of collaboration, sometimes I couldn’t help but wonder if this level of saturation makes it difficult to stand out. How can a joint creation be unique in the age of fast-paced consumption and online fatigue? How effective can partnerships be in the future?

When I attended the recent DigiCon 2026, I discovered that there’s another word for collaboration, but with a richer and clearer structure: Interoperability. At “Interoperability: Welcome to the Age of Collaboration,” the flagship program by the Digital Marketing Association of the Philippines, 2,000 leaders and professionals from the marketing, business, technology, and media industries learned about how this multilayered term means cross-industry collaboration as we tinker with new technologies. Moreover, it happens by bringing out the best in human creativity alongside benefiting from the continuous evolution of AI – not as a replacement, but a collaborator.

One of the speakers, “Connect the Dots” author Dr. Christian Busch, offered an example of this through his talk on serendipity. According to him, the difference between serendipity and luck is that the former is about having agency in what’s going to happen next.

blocks.caption: CHANCE ENCOUNTERS. Dr. Christian Busch talked about the value of unexpected ideas in cultivating effective collaborations

blocks.text: We can study serendipity through interoperability, as we find the unknown connections that can bring us to fruitful situations – and this can be achieved through placing “hooks”. Simply put, these can start with the kind of questions we ask people, like, “What are you currently curious about?” or “What are you currently working on?”
DigiCon co-chair Raymund Sison described interoperability as “one of the most natural things in the world.”

blocks.caption: ALL HANDS ON DECK. DigiCon co-chair Raymund Sison emphasized the need for collective integration in the rise of AI in the digital space

blocks.text: “The earliest forms of large-scale digital interoperability weren’t built for business or entertainment – they were forged by the military and early researchers to ensure that critical data wouldn’t get trapped in a single silo during a crisis. It’s about survival,” he said. “To build a resilient digital economy, we must move beyond individual capabilities and focus on collective integration.”

Empowering people’s potential is important in the event, as DigiCon co-chair Shayne Madamba acknowledges the risk of AI’s takeover of our lives. “Looking at marketing today, paradoxically speaking, as we enter the height of AI where algorithms can hyper-personalize, automate, and even segment faster than ever. Our country, our industry, everyone in this room – we’re actually becoming more fragmented.”

blocks.caption: CRITICAL MINDS. DigiCon co-chair Shayne Madamba grounded the audience by reminding them on the risks of AI’s takeover in the marketing industry

blocks.text: She added, “If we allow it further, AI can build walls of data silos, isolating us, our tools, our channels, and our whole humanity. This is why interoperability is no longer just a buzzword. It is a marketing imperative.”

This year’s two-day DigiCon was divided into Innovation, Integrated, Impact, Immersive, and Interactive tracks. We got to listen to how various companies and brands define interoperability through their lived experiences – some of them, quite unexpected.
Interoperability means integrating with technology – which is common in the workplace. Thus, it’s a must to be responsible with the use of AI.

During the panel discussion, “Privacy and Data Ethics: How to Build a Culture of Responsible AI Inside Your Organization,” Don Kevin Hapal, Rappler’s Chief Data Officer, shared the importance of taking accountability in using AI.

“At the end of the day, if you generated it, you’re still liable for it. Because if something goes wrong because of the content you generated, you cannot suddenly just blame the AI for it. Because at the end of the day, it was you who decided to create that content.”

Hapal emphasized the weight of this in the context of responsible AI use in media. “The responsibility [and] accountability [are] higher if you choose to put it out into public. For example, on social media. You decided to post this information. Because at the end of the day, it doesn’t matter if it’s AI-generated – if you choose to put it out to the public. It’s carrying your name.”

During the talk of Javier Miguel “Javi” Benitez, chairperson of the House Special Committee on Creative Industries and Performing Arts, he emphasized how recent successes in our popular media often started with a “Pwede pala” (So it’s possible) thought. Think of the collaboration of previous rival networks that brought out the country’s highest-grossing film, and even the gradual worldwide rise of our underdogs SB19 and BINI.

Referencing the earlier talk, he emphasized that serendipity can’t work without the proper rails, so interoperability can happen in the form of rights, money, data, talent, and stages, among other forms of support.

On the topic of pop culture, DigiCon also highlighted fandoms as another example of interoperability in play. Ina Flores, founder of fandom platform Hey Roomie, emphasized how fans stay in fandoms because of the community they provide. It’s interoperability at work because what’s happening isn’t passive. Ellen Manalang, leader of OPM artist Maki’s fandom Zushis Official, cited an example: Maki encourages his fans to discuss his work with him, like building a lore together.
Ultimately, interoperability brings us closer together – an important aspect to preserve in the age of AI.

Frances Cabatuando of Home Buddies PH – which houses millions of active members – brought up the value of finding a “north star” for your community. This allows people to know how to utilize the space themselves; they know how to act because they see the group’s purpose. And in big communities, people also get the initiative to create smaller, closer, and more intimate communities. They move on their own.
“You are one idea away from changing the world,” said Judy John, global chief creative officer at Edelman.

blocks.caption: INSPIRING ROOM. Edelman global chief creative officer Judy John, an influential leader in today’s creative industry, graced the event as a keynote speaker

blocks.text: While we’re often hounded by the “doom and gloom” image of the future, interoperability can be one of our strengths, as this inspires mobilization. We don’t just let things unfold. We’re aware that we can still make things happen the way we want to, if we’re brave enough to operate collectively. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
articles.summary: As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests…

image.caption: China and Russia back Iran but must balance that support against broader interests with WashingtonImage: Mandel Ngan/AFP

blocks.text: As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.
For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow.

Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran. But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.
That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate?
Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit
China is now Iran's economic lifeline
China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil.
In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions.
As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs.
Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own.

"If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW.
But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter.
"The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said.
Sanctions enforcement raises pressure on Iran
That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports.

In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny.
As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets.
"A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said.
Iran prepares for the worst
This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning.
A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero.

That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks.

Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating.
What does Beijing want?
Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost.
But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies.
A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping. China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability.
Russia can help, but how much?

Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation. Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.

blocks.caption: Trump, Xi and Putin each seek to advance competing interests on Iran, Ukraine, trade and international securityImage: Sergey Bobylev/SNA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East.
"Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW.
Russia supports Iran, but limits remain
Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran.
The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf.
Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost.
"Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he said.
Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine.
How much influence do the three powers have?
For Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran.

Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington.

articles.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
articles.summary: Some local media report that at least four bodies have been recovered.

blocks.text: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.
Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.

As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

articles.title: It's costing you less to fill up your gas tank. What's behind falling pump prices?

image.caption: A man fuels up at a gas station in Surrey, British Columbia, on Friday, Mar. 13, 2026. Drivers across Canada will be paying less to fill their tanks this week, thanks to easing tensions in Iran and seasonal factors that are causing gas prices to dip. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

While gas prices are still higher than they were a year ago, a litre of gas will cost you nearly 30 cents less than it did a month ago, based on national average prices. A mix of seasonal factors and more oil moving out of the Middle East are to thank, according to analysts.
National average gas prices 29.4 cents below the national average from 30 days ago
No, your eyes aren't deceiving you — those sky-high gas prices are coming down across Canada.

The Canadian national average for gas prices sat at $1.514 per litre as of Wednesday, according to price tracking site affordableenergy.ca. That's down about eight cents compared to a week ago, and 29.4 cents below the national average from 30 days ago, according to the tracking site.
In some provinces like Manitoba and Saskatchewan, those average prices are down by more than 30 cents compared to last month's average, according to GasBuddy petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan.
"In fact, in some areas of Calgary, we are seeing gas stations … below a dollar a litre again," De Haan said.

He says prices could still fall by another five or 10 cents a litre countrywide over the next few weeks — so long as there are no new developments with the U.S. war in Iran, which at some points all but shuttered traffic through the vital Strait of Hormuz, sending oil skyrocketing.
While gas prices are still higher than they were a year ago, they have recently been brought down largely due to more oil moving through the strait, as well as some seasonal factors, analysts say.

Tanker traffic through the strait has been ticking up in recent months, aided by U.S. military escorts through the waterway, according to Al Salazar, head of oil and gas research at Enverus. That has helped crude oil prices come down — a barrel of Brent crude oil is now priced just under $92 US, compared to about $116 US at a high point in mid-October.

Gas prices are pictured at 222.9¢ a litre at a gas station in New Westminster, B.C., on May 1. The oil shock brought on by the war in Iran has sent gas prices way up in recent months, in some cases far past $2 a litre. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
"The U.S. military, prior to the midterms, was really [helping] improve and defend the ships getting through the strait. So that's led to a bit of a glut," Salazar said.
The International Energy Agency also said last week that the world oil market could return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, as more oil is able to make it out of the Middle East.

Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump himself has taken a de-escalatory tone on the war. And expectations that Democrats could use their newfound power picked up in the midterms to block new strikes on Iran, encouraging oil prices to fall lower, Salazar said.
Seasonal factors are also giving the industry a lot of "breathing room," according to De Haan.

The seasonal switch to the cheaper "winter blend" gas is in effect, and refinery maintenance associated with the swap is wrapping up. Maintenance at the Irving Oil plant in New Brunswick was slated to finish yesterday, while De Haan adds that more production at refineries in the prairies is contributing to the big pump price drops in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel
There's also the fact that Canadians tend to drive less in the winter as they hunker down in the colder months, helping with demand.

And while the cost of diesel — which had been pressuring industries like trucking, farming and fishing — has also eased, relief on that front might be more short-lived, said Dan McTeague, president of the Canadians for Affordable Energy lobby group.

items: The price of diesel is skyrocketing. Here's why Canadians may soon feel it at the grocery store

blocks.text: Diesel is similar to jet fuel and home heating oil — and the latter will be in higher demand as temperatures drop heading into winter, McTeague said.
"[With] diesel, this is probably as good as it's going to get at the end of this week," he told CBC's Hanomansing Live earlier this week.
Gas prices have dropped across Canada — how long will it last? | Hanomansing Live

De Haan predicts lower gasoline prices will last into early 2027, but notes some of that "artificial drop" will disappear when the suspended fuel excise tax comes back. The tax will return at a 50 per cent rate at the end of January 2027, before returning to its full amount at the end of March.

And, De Haan and Salazar both say costs could always soar again if tensions flare with Iran. Especially since strikes on ships in the strait have already risen again over the past few days, Salazar expects the relief at the pump might not last long.

items: Iran and U.S. trade fire as Iran denies reports of planned dirty bomb attack in D.C.

blocks.text: "It really is a war call. And for us, it just doesn't seem like there's a durable solution to preventing the Iranians from attacking ships," Salazar said.
"So take the swoon in prices to your advantage temporarily, but I suspect that we're going to have higher prices to come still."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, held in Manila from November 15 to 18, became a showdown between activists protesting the planned local construction of data centers under the US-led Pax Silica initiative, and police tasked with maintaining order as the Marcos Jr. administration hosts world leaders including US President Donald Trump.
