articles.title: Skipping work to play Grand Theft Auto VI? You're not alone
articles.summary: Got IT problems at work? Call somebody else. Need to develop some corporate training? It'll have to wait until next week. That's because many video game fans are taking time off to play the…

image.caption: The video game Grand Theft Auto VI is being released on Thursday after a long wait, and many gamers are planning to take time off to play it. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Got IT problems at work? Call somebody else. Need to develop some corporate training? It'll have to wait until next week. That's because many video game fans are taking time off to play the highly-anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI that comes out Thursday. HR experts say it's far from the first cultural event to have people skipping work.
Fans take time off, call in sick and even buy new gaming systems in anticipation of video game's release
Got IT problems at work? Call somebody else. Need to develop some corporate training? It'll have to wait until next week.

Gabriel Santaguida and Amberley Houseman, a Montreal couple who work as a systems administrator and e-learning specialist, respectively, would normally take care of such things, but they're taking the next two days off work to play the long-awaited video game Grand Theft Auto VI that finally arrives Thursday.
"It actually started as a joke, because Gabriel had said, 'Oh, it would be funny if we took the day off for something like this,'" said Houseman.
"Then I was like, 'Wait, I think I'm picking up what you're putting down.'"
Houseman and Santaguida aren't alone. Many fans are gearing up to play the open-world action adventure video game that lets players commit a wide array of crimes as they explore the fictional world.

Montreal couple Gabriel Santaguida, 28, and Amberley Houseman, 29, who enjoy video games like Stardew Valley, are both taking two days off work to play Grand Theft Auto VI when it's released on Thursday. (Submitted by Gabriel Santaguida)

A survey by U.S. HR company BambooHR polled 1,530 employed adults in the U.S. between Oct. 9-20. It also looked at data from approved and pending paid time off requests filed on their platform by about 575,000 active employees at Canadian companies from 2024 to 2026.

It found that time-off requests were up 13 per cent in the United States and up 6.6 per cent in Canada for Thursday compared to equivalent days last year, though respondents didn't make a direct connection to the game's release.

items: Grand Theft Auto VI means Surrey landscaping company employees get the day off
GTA fever expected to cause sick leaves, absences as gamers gear up for launch day

blocks.text: The survey also found that of those who intended to take time off for an upcoming video game release, 50 per cent were planning to call in sick rather than schedule time off.
Some employers are just giving in.
Grand Theft Auto VI-mania hits Canada

Tech company Logitech is giving its 7,000 employees a paid day off Friday so they can play the game, while game developer Pocket Pair announced a five-day holiday for its gamer employers. Edison Motors, the Canadian electric truck company based out of B.C., announced employees could take the two days off, though they would be unpaid.

"Everybody's got their thing that they're going to take time off for, and for some people it's gaming," said Tara Parry, director of permanent services with human resources consulting firm Robert Half Canada.
"We shouldn't shun them for that, we should find a way to embrace it and get people to be upfront about it."
Why the hype?
Grand Theft Auto VI allows players to control Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval in the fictional U.S. state of Leonida, modelled after Florida.

Like previous iterations of the game, players can steal cars, rob stores and get up to all sorts of other mischief, but it also lets them do simple things such as pet cats and hold hands with their in-game partner.
Gamers get to play as Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval in the fictional U.S. state of Leonida. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
"This is really a historic franchise. One of the biggest in gaming," said Bradly Shankar, gaming editor at the tech news website MobileSyrup in Mississauga, Ont.

Grand Theft Auto V — which was released on Sept. 17, 2013 — has sold over 235 million copies, according to its publisher Take-Two Interactive, which owns Rockstar Games. At launch it made $800 million US, and just a few days following its release, it hit $1 billion US.
Thirteen years later, Grand Theft Auto VI has already made $1.5 billion US in pre-sales, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

items: Grand Theft Auto VI is a spectacular, cynical and sometimes shallow joyride through the American psyche
GTA VI in the GTA? Man builds Grand Theft Auto-inspired video game set in Toronto

blocks.text: For Houseman and Santaguida, it wasn't as simple as just pre-ordering the game and clicking download. They had played Grand Theft Auto V on PC, but the new game isn't available on that platform at launch.
"We did actually buy a PlayStation 5 just to play this game. And it's been sitting in the living room ever since," said Santaguida.
With the price of the game and Playstation 5, he estimates it cost about $1,000. But he was able to use credit card points to pay for the gaming system.
GTA VI is an 'astonishing' open world, but no revolution in gaming, says CBC reviewer
Adjusting to the trend
Parry, with Robert Craft Canada, says Grand Theft Auto VI is far from the first major cultural event to have people skipping work or using vacation days.
She says millions of Americans either booked off or called in sick the Monday after the 2026 Superbowl, which she says equated to billions of dollars in lost productivity
"We aren't anticipating that level of impact with Grand Theft Auto, but it does have a meaningful impact."

items: Should bosses let employees watch the World Cup at work?
More employees skipping work after big sports events like the Super Bowl, poll finds

blocks.text: But, she says businesses could be acknowledging how workers are taking part in these events rather than denying that they're happening.
"Why not embrace it and incorporate it into the corporate environment for Thursday, Friday. Call it what it is, maybe set it up so people are gaming in office as opposed to home alone," she said.

This screenshot shows Brian Heder, a character from Grand Theft Auto VI. Tara Parry says employers should prepare for and embrace cultural events such as the release of the new game. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
In Canada, Parry says many businesses set up watch parties for employees during the FIFA 2026 World Cup, especially for Canada games.
"Most employers recognize that when Team Canada was playing, productivity was going to grind to a halt. So rather than deny it or fight against it, a lot of companies leaned into it," she said.

items: Vancouver duo's song goes viral after featuring in Grand Theft Auto VI
Is Grand Theft Auto VI the most anticipated video game of all time?

blocks.text: While Houseman and Santaguida had to use their own personal days off, they say when they finally sit down to play Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday morning, it will be a rare chance to preserve some time just for fun.
"When you become an adult with adult responsibilities, then I think the moments to just be a kid are a little more rare. And so we take them where we can get them," said Houseman.
"I think we both know it's a little silly," said Santaguida. "But that's also kind of the fun, right?"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Philip Drost is a network senior writer for CBC News based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.
With files from Makda Ghebreslassie and Olivia Zhong

articles.title: Juliet Daniel changed cancer research. Students of the late Canadian scientist say she also changed lives
articles.summary: Friends, students and colleagues gathered this week at McMaster University in Hamilton to celebrate Juliet Daniel, a Barbadian-Canadian professor and scientist who died April 28 at age 61. They…

image.caption: Juliet Daniel, a Barbadian-Canadian professor, scientist and community advocate, was 61 when she passed away on April 28. (Submitted by Juliet Daniel)

blocks.text: Shaiya Robinson saw something she hadn't seen before — a Black woman leading a cancer research lab — when she was a student and first met Juliet Daniel at McMaster University for an interview in 2009.
Robinson, who had rarely encountered Black professors, said the meeting to join the lab was about more than an interview. It was the first time she could picture herself in that position.
"I'd never had a Black professor before."
Daniel became her supervisor, mentor and, eventually, a colleague.
Now, Robinson is an assistant professor at McMaster, carrying forward many of the lessons she learned from the woman who helped make that future possible.

Robinson was among former students, friends and colleagues who gathered Monday at McMaster University to honour the legacy of Daniel. The Barbadian-Canadian professor and scientist was a longtime breast cancer survivor who died on April 28 at age 61.
"She was such a pivotal person in every step of my career journey and my personal journey," Robinson recalled.
Determined to ask different questions
Daniel joined McMaster in November 1999 as an assistant professor, becoming the first Black woman faculty member in the university's faculty of science.
Her research focused on understanding why certain cancers impact some populations more than others, and why outcomes can differ.
She was internationally recognized for her research into triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), an aggressive form of the disease that disproportionately affects Black and Hispanic women.

Her work helped advance understanding of the genetic differences behind cancer outcomes, including her discovery of a gene she named Kaiso, after a style of calypso music rooted in her Caribbean heritage.
Michele James knew Daniel for about 30 years and sits on the board of The Olive Branch of Hope (TOBOH), a breast cancer support organization.
James said Daniel was looking into health equity and reducing health-care disparities long before it became a mainstream conversation.
"She was a real trailblazer in that regard."

Daniel co-founded organizations including the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster, the Canadian Black Scientists Network, the McMaster Academic Women’s Success and Mentorship Lecture Series, and the Canadian Multicultural LEAD Organization for Mentoring and Training. (Paul Smith/CBC)
Made time for students, community
Robinson said Daniel had a demanding schedule, but somehow always made students and colleagues feel they had her full attention.
"She didn't have time, but she always made you feel like there was time for you."
Daniel also mentored Kevin Kelly, who now works in biotechnology.

Kelly met Daniel in 2000, when he was an undergraduate student looking for a supervisor for his research project. He stayed in her lab through his PhD, becoming the first doctoral graduate from her research group.
Kelly said Daniel was someone who took mentorship seriously and was generous with her time.
"She was always thinking about her students."
He said he admired her willingness to pursue questions that drew little scientific attention, particularly around cancer in Black women.
Kevin Kelly and Dr. Shaiya Robinson, left to right, were both mentored by Daniel. They remember her for her scientific accomplishments and compassionate style of mentoring. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)

Daniel also helped build a stronger community for Black academics. She co-founded the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster and the Canadian Black Scientists Network, along with several other initiatives supporting mentorship, inclusion and student success.

"I was really proud of her for taking that very courageous step," James said. "She was already busy and that was something else that she took on to help advance things not for herself, but for the other faculty members."
Proud to be Bajan
For Stephanie Roberts, Daniel was first and foremost a childhood friend.

The two grew up in the same neighbourhood in Barbados, meeting when Roberts was about three and Daniel was five. They remained close even after Daniel moved to Canada and Roberts immigrated to the United States.
Roberts recalled Daniel's determination to make a difference in cancer research, particularly after her mother died of the disease.
She said Daniel initially pursued medicine before choosing research as a way to help find better answers for people affected by cancer.
"It was never about the money," Roberts said. "She truly wanted a cure for cancer."

items: To confront race in Canada, she became a beauty queen, a tour guide and a time traveller

blocks.text: Although they were in different job fields, Daniel would sometimes invite Roberts to tag along on work trips.
She also remembers Daniel as a longtime friend from her home country.
Daniel loved calypso music, dancing, cooking and hosting friends, and was an accomplished ballroom dancer who won several awards, Roberts said.
She said Daniel never made a point of introducing herself by her title, despite her academic achievements.
"If you went anywhere with her, she always went and said, 'Hi, I'm Juliet.'"
Pioneering cancer researcher wants more diversity in STEM fields
Roberts says Daniel was always proud to be from Barbados and would do whatever she could to give back.
James said Daniel helped the island during the COVID-19 pandemic by connecting its government with people who could facilitate access to vaccines, medical expertise and supplies.

Daniel's contributions earned her numerous honours, including being named a Distinguished University Professor in 2025, McMaster's highest recognition for faculty members. Her research has been cited more than 6,400 times.
In 2024, the federal government's Canadian Intellectual Property Office named Daniel as one of three Black Innovators in Research and Medicine.
Roberts hopes Daniel's name will be permanently recognized, including at a potential tribute at McMaster and possibly seeing Barbados's living lab named after her.
"It's just sad that in most cases, we have to wait on some till someone passes to celebrate them."
Robinson said she wants to continue Daniel's example by making mentorship a priority for her own students.
The event to honour Daniel drew friends, colleagues, students and mentees to the McLean Centre for Collaborative Discovery at McMaster University. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)
During Monday's celebration, James shared a quote that she said captured Daniel's approach to life: "It's better to light one small candle than to curse the darkness."
James noted that the celebration drew many people whose lives were touched by Daniel.
"She was like a candle that you can just take that candle and use it to light lots and lots of other candles," she said.
"And as I looked out into the room this afternoon, I felt that there were so many candles that had been lit initially by Juliet, and that their light would carry on indefinitely."

For more stories about the experiences of Black Canadians — from anti-Black racism to success stories within the Black community — check out Being Black in Canada, a CBC project Black Canadians can be proud of. You can read more stories here.
(CBC)

articles.title: VIA Rail heading back to Quebec’s Gaspé region after 15 years — a partial win that brings hope
articles.summary: Gaspé residents who have been waiting for the return of passenger train service since 2011 hope new federal investments and commitments from VIA Rail will lead to full service resumption down the…

image.caption: Eileen Jessop said that as a young adult, she could walk to her local train station in Chandler, Que., and get off in downtown Montreal the next morning. (Julia Page/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

Gaspé residents who have been waiting for the return of passenger train service since 2011 hope new federal investments and commitments from VIA Rail will lead to full service resumption down the line.
VIA Rail route to New Carlisle, Que., expected to resume by spring 2028
After 15 years of lobbying for the return of passenger train service to the Gaspé region, residents are finally seeing light at the end of the tunnel.

VIA Rail confirms it will resume partial service along the Baie des Chaleurs, reaching New Carlisle, Que., by spring 2028. This commitment from the Crown corporation paired with a $1.2 billion investment over three years for VIA Rail are fuelling hope full service to the Gaspé region — including the city that bears the same name — could return after a 15-year absence.
But the Quebec government needs to jump on board.

"It's great news in itself," said Éric Dubé, mayor of New Richmond and president of Société du chemin de fer de la Gaspésie (SCFG), a local non-profit organization in charge of repairing and operating the tracks.
The last passenger train reached the city of Gaspé in December 2011, after the tracks were deemed unsafe. In 2013, the final stop became Matapédia, leaving a 325-kilometre stretch without service.
For residents, news of the partial return of passenger train service brings back memories of an era when travelling to and from the Gaspé region was much more accessible.
"Back in the good years of the 1990s, as many as 28,000 passengers a year would take the train to the Gaspé Peninsula — so we’d love to be able to see that happen again someday," said Dubé.
The return of passenger train service to New Carlisle will cut the driving distance in half for travellers headed to Gaspé. (Lorena Suárez del Real/CBC)
The province, which has owned the tracks since 2015, has invested $350 million so far, which enabled the partial return of freight trains to the region.
Until now, VIA Rail was steadfast in its position to only bring back service to the region if the full line was refurbished, said Dubé.
"Before it was [all the way to the city of] Gaspé or nothing. Now they are agreeing to a partial return to New Carlisle, but with the objective the tracks be refurbished all the way to Gaspé."
The final stop for shipping goods is currently near the cement plant in Port-Daniel-Gascons.
VIA Rail’s partial return to Quebec’s Gaspé region — after 15 years — sparks hope

VIA Rail confirmed to CBC by e-mail the service between Quebec City and New Carlisle would run two to three times a week in a "phased return of service," while "working with the government of Quebec, infrastructure owners, local communities and all partners involved to move this important project forward."
Rail crucial for access to health care, local businesses

Dubé hopes the next provincial budget will include money to repair the last section of tracks between Port-Daniel-Gascons and Gaspé. That is also an ongoing demand from the local citizens' committee that has been at the forefront of the battle to bring back the train.
Residents on the Gaspé peninsula have been campaigning for the return of passenger train service since VIA Rail cut back service in 2011. (Julia Page/CBC)
"It's really disappointing to see how much the service has degraded in my lifetime," said Eileen Jessop, with the Coalition pour le retour des services d'un train de passagers en Gaspésie.

Jessop said going to see a show or visit family in Montreal used to be as simple as walking to the station in Chandler to board a night train. Now travelling back and forth to Matapedia adds on hours of driving.
"It's rough on the roads, it's rough on our vehicles, it's rough on our mental health."

items: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like in much of the country, it's not so simple

blocks.text: Many people who live in the region, including seniors, don't have access to a car, said Jessop, and often need to travel to Quebec City or Montreal to see medical specialists. The coalition also wants the province and VIA rail to arrange for more comfortable wagons designed for health care transportation.
Quebec’s new Transport Minister Nicolas Girard said there were no new developments for the moment, but his office said "an update could be made further down the line."

After numerous announcements from the province over the years to finalize repairs on the tracks, the project was sent back to the 'planning stage' in Quebec's 2025 infrastructure plan. (Julia Page/CBC)
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Transport "continues to work with VIA Rail with the aim of a resumption of passenger service," Girard's office said in a statement.
For Jessop, if rail service comes back, she wants to tick travelling from Gaspé to Vancouver off her bucket list.
"If the train comes back that's going to be one of my first things — taking the Canadian to the other side."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Julia Page is a radio and online journalist with CBC News, based in Quebec City. Her role is to travel to communities across the province, from Gaspé to Trois-Rivières to Rouyn-Noranda, to meet with Quebecers and reflect the issues affecting their communities. She can be reached at julia.page@cbc.ca.

articles.title: AI potential as economic growth source among Marcos' agenda in APEC
articles.summary: Malacañang said the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) as a driver of economic growth is on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr."s agenda at this year"s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC)…

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 4:54pm

Malacañang said the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) as a driver of economic growth is on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s agenda at this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in China.

In an interview with Balitanghali on Thursday, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the Philippines aims to deepen its engagement in AI and ensure the country does not fall behind in its evolving technology.

“Isa talaga sa target ng Pangulo ay magkaroon ng paglago sa ekonomiya ng bansa. Kailangan natin maipakita kung ano ang kakayahan ng Pilipinas, kung maaari silang, paano silang dapat dito rin mag-invest sa Pilipinas,” Castro said.
(One of the President’s main targets is to generate economic growth for the country. We need to showcase what the Philippines is capable of and demonstrate how and why they should invest here.)
“At ang isa sa mga tinututukan ng Pangulo dito ay 'yung technological change, particularly 'yung AI as a new source of growth,” she added.
(One of the key areas the President is focusing on is technological change, particularly AI as a new source of growth.)
Aside from technology and investments, the Palace said Marcos will also focus on agriculture, education, and trade during his meetings.
Marcos arrived in China on Wednesday to participate in the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting.
The meetings will run from November 18 to 19, following the annual APEC CEO Summit held from November 17 to 18.
Also present at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting are US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Tusk appears to mock Trump’s Putin comment as Ukraine’s allies meet in Berlin – Europe live
articles.summary:
After US president called Putin a friend, Poland’s PM said: ‘God, protect us from such friends’

On Ukraine, Trump says at the beginning of the trilateral…

blocks.text: 'God, protect us from such friends,' Poland's Tusk says after Trump's 'he's my friend' comments to Putin
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.
“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:

“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern. Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”
Key events

items: 12m ago'We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine,' Trump says
14m ago'Together we are making history,' Trump declares as trilateral with Putin, Xi gets under way
17m ago'God, protect us from such friends,' Poland's Tusk says after Trump's 'he's my friend' comments to Putin
18m agoMorning opening: Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin, anxious to hear about Trump's meeting with Putin, Xi

blocks.text: 'We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine,' Trump says
On Ukraine, Trump says at the beginning of the trilateral meeting:

“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That’s what pretty much what the discussion was about. And I think things are happening. I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war.”
God knows what that’s supposed to mean in practice.
'Together we are making history,' Trump declares as trilateral with Putin, Xi gets under way

The trilateral meeting is now getting under way, with Trump declaring “together we are making history” with the three leaders facing “a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet.”

blocks.caption: Putin, Xi and Trump Photograph: Win McNamee/Reuters

blocks.text: Our coverage of the Apec summit is here, but I will pick up any lines on Ukraine:
Morning opening: Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin, anxious to hear about Trump's meeting with Putin, Xi

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Several European leaders from the Coalition of the Willing are meeting in Berlin today, just hours after US president Donald Trump, Russia president Vladimir Putin and China president Xi Jinping are due to meet in Shenhzen.
The trilateral meeting is due to get under way any moment now, though the tone of Trump’s earlier talks with Putin will already be worrying for Europeans.

blocks.caption: Loop: Trump and Putin shake hands

blocks.text: “Who is he? He’s my friend!” said Trump, absolutely beaming, as soon as he saw Putin.
These images will send a shiver down the spine of Europe’s top leaders as they prepare to leave for Berlin to attend the “coalition of the willing”’s latest coordination meeting.

blocks.caption: Police officers provide security ahead the summit of the so-called Coalition of the Willing group of pro-Ukrainian countries in Berlin. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

blocks.text: Europe’s newly appointed negotiating team of Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni, Friedrich Merz and Donald Tusk plus the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa will be joined by several other leaders for a meeting with US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, where they are expected to get a read out from the meeting in China.

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte are expected to attend, as are several other key European leaders, including Finland’s Alexander Stubb, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen, Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre, and Ireland’s Micheál Martin (and many others).
I will bring you all the latest from Berlin and reactions to Trump’s trilateral meeting.
It’s Thursday, 19 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: All minors apprehended over ASEAN Summit protest released from custody
articles.summary: All minors who were apprehended at a protest during the ASEAN Summit 2026 opening on Sunday have been released on Thursday, according to Gabriela Women's Party

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 4:38pm
All minors who were apprehended at a protest during the ASEAN Summit 2026 opening on Sunday have been released on Thursday, according to Gabriela Women's Party
Gabriela said in a 2 p.m. update that all of the 15 remaining minors were discharged from the facility on Thursday.
Former Gabriela Women's Party representative Arlene Brosas, lawyers, church workers, and family members were present to welcome the minors and ensure their safe release, the party said.
The release came after families and supporters repeatedly called for the minors' freedom.
Before the release, the National Union of Peoples' Lawyers (NUPL) earlier said that seven minors were still in custody as of Thursday morning.
The lawyers’ group disputed the Department of Justice's (DOJ) previous announcement that all 20 minors arrested in connection with the “Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan” had been released.
NUPL also welcomed the initial release of 216 protesters and journalists from Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City and five other minors from Bahay Pag-asa.
The Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office had ordered the release of the ASEAN Summit 2026 protesters from detention and custody on Wednesday.
In Manila, meanwhile, a total of nine individuals in ASEAN Summit rallies are still under police custody, according to progressive groups on Thursday. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo questions credibility of defense team's witness: Is he a super witness?
articles.summary: Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo on Thursday questioned the credibility of the witness presented by Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team, saying that he's answering questions even outside of his…

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 4:30pm

Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo on Thursday questioned the credibility of the witness presented by Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team, saying that he's answering questions even outside of his expertise.

On the 44th day of the impeachment trial against the Vice President, the defense panel presented Rainer dela Fuente of AML Consulting PH. He was expected to testify on matters in relation to the Anti-Money Laundering Act and other other related documents.
However, Tulfo seemed bothered with the line of questioning and response between defense lawyer Mark Vinluan and Dela Fuente.

"Is he a super witness, omni witness? Ano bang klaseng witness itong pinepresent ng defense? Pati ba naman amici curiae, pakikialaman niya. Supreme Court... Ombudsman... DOJ... Who is he? Who is this guy?" the senator-judge asked.

(Is he a super witness, omni witness? What kind of witness is the defense presenting? Even amici curiae, he's getting involved in that. Supreme Court... Ombudsman... DOJ... Who is he? Who is this guy?)

"I'm really very, very curious about the qualification of this gentleman para lahat ng topic ay kaya niyang sagutin mula sa kanyang handler, or excuse me, sa defense. I don't think he's capable of answering those questions kasi hindi niya na teritoryo 'yun," Tulfo added.

(I'm really very, very curious about the qualification of this gentleman so that he can answer every topic coming from his handler, or excuse me, from the defense. I don't think he's capable of answering those questions because that's no longer his territory.)
Likewise, Senator-judge Joel Villanueva also shared the same sentiments towards the witness.

"Bagat maaari siyang magbigay ng expert opinion sa kanyang larangan bilang eksperto sa money laundering, hindi naman po siya siguro pwede mag-deklara na mali o invalid yung findings ng AMLA at nasa korte yung pagpapasya kung gaano kabigat yung ebidensya na nilalahad dito," he said.

(Although he may be able to give an expert opinion in his field as an expert on money laundering, he probably shouldn't be declaring that the AMLA's findings are wrong or invalid, and it's up to the court to decide how much weight the evidence presented here carries.)
However, Senator-judge Imee Marcos said that her colleagues must understand how justice should work for both parties.

"Ipapaalala ko lang sa lahat na si Lady Justice o yung babaeng hustisya ay bulag, nakatakip ang mata. Kasi hindi kinakailangan na basahin ng bawat dokumento, alamin ang bawat personalidad dahil pantay-pantay ang timbang sa batas," she said.

(I just want to remind everyone that Lady Justice—or the woman of justice—is blind, her eyes are covered. Because it's not necessary to read every document or know every personality, since the scales under the law are equal.)

While he understands the sentiments of Tulfo and Villanueva, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero said that senator-judges should exercise "more leeway, patience" with the defense panel's presentation.

"We note the manifestations made by all the senator-judges. However, the court cannot dictate nor impinge upon how either party will present their evidence much less dictate their strategy in choosing their respective witnesses. I urge our colleagues to exercise more leeway and patience with the presentation being made by the counsel for the respondent," said Escudero.
But Escudero also told the defense panel to take note of the concerns raised by the senator-judges.

"I ask for the indulgence of our colleagues and ask Atty. Mark to take note of the manifestations made and be sensitive to them to a certain extent in continuing with the direct examination of this witness," said Escudero. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: PH envoy Babe Romualdez stresses no data centers eyed in New Clark City
articles.summary: Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel "Babe" Romualdez reiterated on Thursday that no data centers will be built under the US-led Pax Silica initiative in Clark, noting that they are…

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 4:18pm

Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel "Babe" Romualdez reiterated on Thursday that no data centers will be built under the US-led Pax Silica initiative in Clark, noting that they are now calling the projects as a "manufacturing hub" rather than "Pax Silica."
“Wala naman pinag-uusapan na data center na igaganap diyan sa Pax Silica eh. So ‘yung Pax Silica is a manufacturing hub for critical [minerals],” Romualdez said on Super Radyo dzBB.
(There has never been any discussion about setting up a data center under Pax Silica. Instead, Pax Silica is a manufacturing hub for critical minerals.)
“Actually we’re not even calling it Pax Silica, it's more of a development, manufacturing hub that will have not only US companies, but other companies rin,” he added.

The envoy said critical minerals like nickel, which the Philippines typically exports raw and at low prices to China, can now be processed and diversified inside the hub, giving them significantly higher market value.
Citing his discussions with Finance Secretary Frederick Go, Romualdez said data centers were never part of the Pax Silica plans.

“Eh hindi naman natin pwedeng ilagay [ang data centers] sa Clark dahil that is already an economic zone that is already we’re putting manufacturing potentials there and other aspects of our economy is going to be located in the Clark Economic Zone,” Romualdez said.
(We cannot put data centers in Clark because that is already an economic zone where we are placing manufacturing facilities and other key sectors of our economy.)
“So wala sa usapan yang mga ganiyan na data centers (Data centers are really not part of the plan),” he added.
The Pax Silica initiative drew protests from various groups across the country ahead of US President Donald Trump’s state visit to the Philippines earlier this week.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton had previously clarified that no signing of the Pax Silica agreement was scheduled during Trump’s visit.
The Pax Silica initiative is a US-led effort to build a network of allied supply chains for critical technologies and minerals, which the Philippines will host in New Clark City in Tarlac.

Government officials have clarified that there will be no data centers included in the Pax Silica initiative, as its main objective is to process the country’s minerals and manufacture high-tech components for semiconductors and artificial intelligence. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: EDF snaps up 1.3m more customers after Utilita takeover
articles.summary:
Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier

EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than…

blocks.text: EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita.

Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed.
The pair will continue to serve their customers independently until the deal concludes. Utilita customers will be contacted about any changes to their service.
After the deal, EDF has promised to continue to operate from Utilita’s headquarters near Southampton which is the base for about 600of Utilita’s employees.

EDF, which is owned by the French state, set out the takeover plans a year after it completed a deal to take on 47,000 standard credit accounts from Utilita which said it hoped to sharpen its focus on smart pay-as-you-go customers.

The deal is likely to have helped bolster Utilita’s financial position, which briefly fell short of the industry regulator Ofgem’s tougher new financial resilience tests in an industry assessment in September 2025.

Utilita confirmed that it was one of five suppliers which had failed to meet Ofgem’s financial rules last year, but said it was able to comply with the standards within months of the regulator’s red flag.

For EDF, the deal will help to bolster its business as most large suppliers continue to lose customers to smaller rivals. EDF lost about 280,000 customer accounts in the year after July 2025, while British Gas, Scottish Power and E.ON were also losing customers. Octopus Energy, the country’s largest supplier, is the only big energy company which has continued to grow its market share.
Utilita was founded in 2003 as a specialist prepay energy supplier, and became the first supplier to install a smart meter in 2008.

Its pioneering approach to smart metering helped the company to modernise pay-as-you-go energy by allowing customers to top-up via an app, website, or by phone rather than visit a corner shop or post office to pay for credit on a plastic card or key.
after newsletter promotion
Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF’s UK business, said Utilita would bring “further expertise” to the supplier, marking “a significant step” in EDF’s ambition to grow its UK customer business.
“Together, we will have the scale and skills to keep developing services and support for the households who rely on us,” Rossi said.
Bill Bullen, the founder of Utilita, said the deal would ensure that Utilita could continue to provide “best-in-class smart prepay solutions to Britain’s households”.

The deal comes as households prepare for a sharp rise in energy bills this winter. On Wednesday, the consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the quarterly industry price cap would jump 26% from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

MANILA, Philippines – Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero flagged a brief fire transition effect that appeared during the livestream of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Thursday, November 19, and reminded Senate staff to be more mindful of broadcast effects.

“We sincerely apologize for the accidental transition effect that appeared during the livestream of the Senate Impeachment Court proceedings today. The incident was due to an unexpected technical issue during the broadcast, which we deeply regret,” the Senate PRIB said.

“The PRIB is currently upgrading its equipment and undergoing retraining and upskilling of its technical staff in a bid to strengthen the quality of broadcast media coverage for the Filipino people,” it added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Trump didn’t issue an arrest warrant against Marcos
articles.summary: No credible report confirms the existence of a supposed warrant, and the video offers no evidence to back up its claim

blocks.text: Claim: US President Donald Trump has issued an arrest warrant against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who is now “wanted among world leaders.”

Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video was posted by the channel “News Update Files” on November 15, as the Philippines began hosting the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit. It is titled, “Ngayon lang! Trump naglabas ng arrest warrant kay Bangag?! Wanted na si Bangag sa mga world leaders?!”
(Just now! Trump issues an arrest warrant against Bangag?! Is Bangag now wanted by world leaders?!)
Its thumbnail shows photos of Marcos and of Trump holding a document stamped “ARREST WARRANT.” Text overlaid on it reads, “Bangag kulong na?! Trump naglabas ng warrant! Buti nga sa’yo! Bangag ka!”
(Will Bangag be jailed?! Trump issues a warrant! Serves you right! You’re high!)
Another photo used in the video includes the text, “ASEAN Summit [canceled]?!”
As of writing, the video has 32,000 views and 3,100 likes.
The facts: No credible media report, US government statement, or court record shows Trump issuing an arrest warrant against Marcos.
The video does not present proof for its claim either. Its content is merely commentary criticizing the Philippines’ hosting of the summit and alleging mismanagement and poor foreign relations.
Additionally, Marcos cannot be arrested while he is president, as he enjoys immunity from suit.

The video surfaced as Trump arrived in Manila on November 17 for a state visit and to participate in the ASEAN-US Special Summit and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue leaders’ summit. On November 18, Marcos welcomed Trump in Malacañang for bilateral talks and a state luncheon.

Trump opened the meeting by calling the Philippines one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific, describing it as “a bond formed in blood.” He said the US is expanding its defense cooperation with the Philippines.

At the luncheon, Trump announced “the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far,” without giving details. Malacañang described it more as “an understanding on economic cooperation, particularly food and energy supply,” and later said that no deal was signed, including the controversial Pax Silica agreement.

The video’s claim about a canceled ASEAN summit is also unfounded. The summit went ahead and wrapped up on November 17, closing the Philippines’ year-long chairmanship of the regional bloc. (READ: ‘Successful’ ASEAN Summit ends with Marcos unable to solve its hardest problems).
Trump’s return: Trump returned to the Philippines after nine years, having last visited in November 2017.
Following his Manila stop, he is now in China for a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Meanwhile, Marcos is also in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: [Pastilan] Huwag mong buhayin ang patay, Sara
articles.summary: An impeachment trial is not a film festival for recycled political grievances. Nor is it an exercise in nostalgia.

blocks.text: An impeachment trial is not a film festival for recycled political grievances. Nor is it an exercise in nostalgia.

The public has waited a long time for Sara Duterte to answer questions about her and her family’s unexplained wealth. On Thursday morning, November 19, the 44th day of her impeachment trial, the defense appeared determined to answer anything but those questions.
What unfolded in the Senate impeachment court was less a demonstration of legal strategy than a spectacle of legal bewilderment.

It was like entering a cooking competition with an empty basket, an empty stove and absolutely nothing cooking, then spending the entire morning showing the judges photographs of meals prepared by other contestants. There was no food, no recipe, and no evidence that they had ever been near a kitchen.

Yet they had a slideshow. They had archival footage. They had pictures of famous chefs looking furious, other contestants crying, and somebody’s grandfather complaining about the previous cooking competition.

Meanwhile, the judges were still waiting for something edible. The contestant, apparently convinced that nostalgia is a culinary technique, kept serving up old photographs and wondering why nobody was impressed. At some point, this stops being a cooking competition and becomes an elaborate demonstration of how to avoid making dinner.

The question before the court is straightforward: Can Sara Duterte account for the wealth attributed to her and her family? At the center of that question are P319 million in foreign remittances allegedly received by Cale88 Foods Corporation, a firm partly owned by her husband. The Anti-Money Laundering Council has testified that the money came from China and Hong Kong. A financial forensic report, meanwhile, has raised questions about the company’s financial statements and whether its reported business activities can explain the movement of money through its accounts. These are specific claims that call for specific answers. The defense cannot make them disappear by discussing something else.
There are concrete allegations that call for concrete answers.

Instead, the defense chose to screen video clips of the late senator Miriam Defensor Santiago, the late former chief justice Renato Corona and Rodrigo Duterte, the vice president’s father and a detained former president.

One clip showed Santiago delivering a blistering lecture to prosecutors during Corona’s impeachment trial. Another featured Corona making an emotional appeal while fighting for his survival as chief justice. The third showed Rodrigo Duterte flatly rejecting suggestions that then vice president Leni Robredo should be impeached.
One might reasonably ask what any of this has to do with the allegations against Sara. The answer, so far, is nothing apparent.

Santiago’s eloquence won’t establish the legitimacy of Cale88’s transactions. Corona’s emotional distress won’t explain the company’s foreign remittances. And Rodrigo Duterte’s position about impeaching Robredo during his presidency won’t constitute evidence that his daughter can account for her wealth.

An impeachment trial is not a film festival for recycled political grievances. Nor is it an exercise in nostalgia. Evidence is supposed to establish or challenge facts relevant to the charges. It is not supposed to provide a convenient occasion for playing old political footage and hoping that the emotional associations will do the work of an argument.

It is difficult to see why the serious questions surrounding Sara’s wealth should be displaced by video clips from entirely different impeachment proceedings, and her father’s pronouncements when he was president. That’s far out.

And what does this say about the lawyers entrusted with defending the vice president? Do they understand the case they are supposed to be answering? Do they appreciate that the impeachment court is not a stage for political theatrics, and that the reputation of a legal team rests on the quality of its arguments rather than the volume of its distractions?

There is something almost self-defeating about a defense that appears to mistake such antics for substance. Every irrelevant exhibit risks reminding the public of the very questions the lawyers and their client have yet to answer.
The defense may believe it is scoring political points. But a lawyer’s job is not to win a partisan audience. It is to confront the evidence.

For now, the defense seems to be laying an egg (read: “nangingitlog”). And the most damaging part may not be what they are failing to prove, but what they are revealing about their own approach to the trial.

The vice president was brought to the impeachment court with allegations of unexplained wealth hanging over her. The public is entitled to expect answers. So far, she has offered none except a collection of old political grievances from another time, a few familiar faces from impeachment history and a defense that seems to have forgotten what game it is playing.Cl

She was quoted by TV5 News on Wednesday, November 18, as saying that corruption “is a progressive disorder that has embedded itself deep within the DNA of the government – and tragically, it is the Filipino people who are left to suffer the consequences.” She urged the public to demand accountability.

I couldn’t agree more. But accountability cannot be a slogan reserved only for one’s political enemies. It must apply even to those who preach against corruption while facing serious questions about their own wealth. Sara cannot demand that the Filipino people hold others accountable while refusing to give them straight answers herself. If accountability means anything, it must begin at home.
And that is precisely why Vice President Sara Duterte needs to go. Pastilan. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines – House leaders refuted a claim made by Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson Paolo Panelo that there have been talks in the lower chamber of postponing or deferring the 2028 elections.

There is no such a plan or proposal that is being pushed by the House leadership,” Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez said on Thursday, November 19.

“I urge all parties to refrain from spreading unverified and baseless claims that only serve to sow confusion and undermine public trust in our democratic institutions. This is nothing but a figment of someone’s imagination,” House suffrage committee chairperson Zia Alonto Adiong added.
Their denials came after Panelo said in a Bilyonaryo News Channel interview that Duterte had received information about a “no-elections” scenario for the 2028 polls.

articles.title: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of exiled Sheikh Hasina’s planned return
articles.summary:
Awami League party called for ⁠nationwide protest on Thursday after the government rejected Hasina’s request for passport

Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by…

blocks.text: Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.

Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday.

Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent ⁠protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter ⁠violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson ⁠said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, ​was set on fire late on ‌Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable ‌substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.

blocks.caption: Fire engulfs the Tungipara police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest after the arrest of activists of the banned Awami League party.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.

During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of ‌vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.

On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops ‌belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses ​were set on fire, authorities said.

Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was ​sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges ⁠over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.

At ​least 37 branches and offices of ​Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or ​attempted fires since 10 November, ‌with 14 more ​attacked since midnight ​on Tuesday, the bank said.

On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

The House prosecution panel on Thursday flagged Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team for its use of video clips of the late senator Miriam Defensor-Santiago and former Chief Justice Renato Corona during the impeachment trial.
"I think it's already a bad taste to present the video clips of the late senator Miriam Defensor Santiago and the late CJ Corona," said Lanao del Sur lawmaker Zia Alonto Adiong in a press briefing.

"It's also an issue of ethical question. To us, it is unethical to present video clips of those who have already departed. Their supposed statements have nothing to do with the current impeachment trial of the Vice President Sara Duterte," he added.
During the 44th day of the impeachment trial against the vice president, the defense team presented video clips of Santiago and Corona during the latter's impeachment trial in 2012.
However, several senator-judges also questioned the relevance of presenting such video clips from the past.
Moreover, the prosecution panel said that the defense team do not have enough evidence to present.

"Parang nakita po natin na parang wala silang maipresentang ebidensya para i-weaken ang kaso ng prosecution. Ang ginagawa lang po nila sa ngayon ay appeal to sympathy tapos nagawa nilang kunin ang video clips ng mga namayapa na," Adiong further said.

(It seems we've seen that they have no evidence to present to weaken the prosecution's case. Right now, all they're doing is appealing to sympathy, and they even managed to use video clips of those who have already passed away.)

The second week of the presentation of evidence of the defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte is expected to feature four witnesses who will testify on the status of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared asset of the Vice President’s husband, Atty. Manases Carpio. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Tammy Shipley was supposed to be monitored in prison. Instead she died after drinking 20L of water
articles.summary:
If the Aboriginal woman had been checked at regular intervals as required, her ‘excess consumption of water’ would have been prevented, inquest finds

• Warning: This article contains…

blocks.text: The death of an Aboriginal woman who collapsed after drinking at least 20 litres of water in a New South Wales prison cell was preventable and the result of systemic failures, a coroner has found.
Tammy Michelle Shipley, 47, died at Silverwater women’s correctional centre on 20 December 2022.
State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan ruled on Thursday that her death was caused by low blood sodium levels resulting from excessive water consumption and complications of schizoaffective disorder.
“I’m confident in finding that Tammy’s death was preventable,” O’Sullivan said.

The mother-of-five had been taken into custody on remand 11 days earlier, after being charged with shoplifting offences, but didn’t disclose her mental health issues to police. Police also didn’t double-check her answers about her health, despite the fact she had attended a police station two weeks earlier and told them she heard her neighbour talking in her head.
O’Sullivan found there had been a missed opportunity to recognise the mental health issues that were present, and to potentially divert Shipley away from the criminal justice system.

When she appeared in a local court over the shoplifting charges the next day, the magistrate was not told she had been refused bail on other charges, so made orders they thought would secure her release.
“There was a clear systems failure,” O’Sullivan found.
Shipley should have been continually monitored – both physically and electronically – after twice attempting self-harm in custody.
It was a serious failure that this had not been done, O’Sullivan said.
“If observations had been carried out at the intervals required, it was likely that Tammy’s excess consumption of water would have been … prevented,” she said.
She deemed it unsatisfactory that Shipley had not been seen by a psychiatrist or mental health nurse at any point during the 11 days before her death.

She added that Shipley should have received medical care from the time she started vomiting, after 10am on the day of her death. Instead, she said, Shipley experienced seizures shortly before noon and was seen lying face down on the floor of her cell around an hour later.
A period of 23 minutes lapsed between when she was first seen lying on the ground and the commencement of resuscitation attempts, which the coroner found was unacceptable.
One corrective services officer had hastily closed the door to her cell after smelling faeces in the room earlier in the day.
“It was completely inappropriate that Tammy, who was known to be suffering a mental health condition, was left in that condition in her cell,” O’Sullivan said.

O’Sullivan made 10 recommendations to NSW police, Corrective Services NSW and Justice Health, including a review of the “austere and depressing” unit in which Shipley was held, which was intended to be a therapeutic space but left the coroner gravely concerned.
after newsletter promotion
She also recommended regular monitoring of footage inside the jail and improved maintenance and cross-checking of records related to mental health conditions.
The coroner acknowledged the jail had already made changes after Shipley’s death.
Outside the court, Shipley’s mother, Vicki, said she hoped the findings would force the system to assess how people are treated.
“I honestly thought that at this stage of our country’s development, we have moved past how convicts were treated,” she said.
“The system – every system – eventually caused trauma to my daughter, until eventually it killed her.”
Vickey Shipley urged the NSW government to quickly implement the recommendations.
“If they’re not made, there will be some other family standing here doing exactly the same thing that I am,” she said.
“All too often we hear the cry: ‘There’s not enough money.’
“How much is a life worth?”

articles.title: Mother whose twin baby died was determined to have home birth despite advice of experts, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into deaths of four babies in northern NSW between 2022 and 2024 told mother refused to give birth in hospital after hearing others’ traumatic stories

  • Get our

blocks.text: Baby B’s mother was so determined to have a home birth she ignored the advice of experts – including her own midwife, an inquest has heard.
The inquest heard she was pregnant with twins, which she described as a “wonderful shock”, and didn’t want a hospital birth because she had heard of others’ traumatic experiences.

The New South Wales coroner’s court in Lismore heard on Thursday that the local medical community in the Hunter Valley swung in to action, warning the mother – who cannot be named for legal reasons – that a home birth was risky while also preparing in case something went wrong.
Baby B died of a bacterial infection, while the other baby got sick but survived.

Baby B’s death is part of an ongoing inquest into the deaths of four babies – Baby R, Baby D, Baby DH and Baby B – who were born in free births or home births in NSW’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.

The first three babies died after a free birth – where no medical professionals are present. By contrast, four midwives were part of the birthing plan for Baby B. The main midwife continued to support the woman.
“The alternative was that she would birth at home with no support whatsoever,” the midwife – whose name is suppressed – told the court.
The court heard that expert opinion found that the midwives’ treatment was “reasonable and appropriate”, which was a clear distinction from the other three births being examined at the inquest.
“It will also be clear from the expert evidence that a home birth was still considered by the experts to be not suitable in the circumstances,” the court heard.

Expert witness, Prof Hannah Dahlen, said that was because it was a twin pregnancy, that it had continued beyond 41 weeks, that there had been no specialist review, that the family were far away from the hospital, and that “there was a possible need for urgent operative birth and the need to provide simultaneous skilled care and resuscitation for two babies”.
But the mother declined multiple checks, and her distrust of the medical system was only reinforced as the pregnancy progressed.
She had scans at 12 weeks and at 22 weeks, but chose not to have hospital antenatal care, or to consult with an obstetrician. A local doctor followed up, but she told them she was doing well.
Her midwife recommended monthly ultrasounds, and induction at 36 to 37 weeks. She declined. The midwife told the court she warned the mother about the risks at every visit.
In evidence read to the court, the mother said she had always planned to have a home birth after hearing traumatic birth stories from other people.
“I did a lot of research and found the midwives, so … I felt comfortable to still home birth the twins,” she said.
She said she was “quite selective” finding midwives with home birth experience and had researched the experience online and in books.

The court heard “a lot of staff” at the local hospital were concerned about the plan, and the ambulance service was worried enough to organise a second paediatric resuscitation kit. There was collaboration and communication between the midwife, obstetricians from the local hospital, and a local GP.
after newsletter promotion
In court, the midwife said the mother wouldn’t have hesitated to seek help if it was needed, and that she thought she could convince the mother to go to hospital, or at least somewhere closer to it.
But then ambulance officers – and later, police – turned up at the home to do a welfare check, making the mother angry, upset, and more determined not to enter the health system.
“She felt quite violated because they came to her home,” the midwife told the court. “They were coercing her to attend the hospital.”
The mother went into labour at home, and the first twin was born successfully. Baby B “gave an initial gasp”, “appeared stunned” and needed help to breathe spontaneously.

Everything seemed to be fine, the court heard. The mother said the next night she could hear the baby breathing, and did not notice any changes. But in the early hours of the morning, Baby B was no longer breathing. When emergency services arrived, they noted that Baby B was “pale, unresponsive and not breathing, with no pulse, although she was still warm to touch”.
Hospital records show continued they continued to work for 45 mins to save her once she arrived there, but she was flatlining. Her blood sugar and temperature were low, and she died.
By that stage, the boy twin was limp and grey. He likely had the same infection but it was less severe, and he survived.
The midwife said she surrendered her registration after the death, both because of its effect on her and because of the way the health system treated her.

She said she wasn’t told when Baby B died. When someone from the hospital rang to ask about the surviving twin, she assumed they were asking about Baby B and asked whether she was being transferred to a bigger hospital.
“Oh, she’ll be going to the coroner,” the midwife was told.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Interview with Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer
articles.summary: Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer speaks about Slovenia-Philippine relations and his country's accession to the ASEAN Treaty of Amity and Cooperation.

blocks.text: An Interview with Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer Cristina Chi Philstar.com Senior Reporter

Minister, thank you once again for accommodating our request. It's really great to meet you and to have you here in Manila. Of course, this week the big thing is that Slovenia is signing ASEAN's peace pact, the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation. What is the significance of this, and what is Slovenia signaling with this, especially amid today's global tensions?

Thank you very much for this opportunity to have me here. Well, for Slovenia, we are, just to start, a country in Central Europe. If people picture the Italian boot, at the top of the boot, a little bit to the right, there is Slovenia.
And the Philippines and Slovenia, we are connected through the sea. We have the Port of Koper. And for the Philippines, Slovenia can be, and I think it's already, a gateway to Central Europe.

And vice versa, we are a highly export-oriented economy. We are 2 million people, and 80% of what we produce, we export. So the majority of the exports go to the European Union, because we are a member of the European Union, but we would like to diversify.

We would like to do more, especially in Southeast Asia and especially with the Philippines. So, to sign this Treaty of Amity and Cooperation, it's opening basically a new avenue for us. And of course, you have to understand that ASEAN and the European Union are two really big associations.

And the trade and cooperation between us, it's really important for both sides. So, hopefully, at the beginning of 2027, that's in January, the so-called FTA, free trade agreement, will be in force, and that is going to even open a new possibility. So, the short answer to your question is, for Slovenia, this is really, really important, and we are looking forward to basically deepening the cooperation with the Philippines.

Minister, you mentioned that we do have very special ties, the Philippines and Slovenia. I'm curious to know, since Manila hosts your only embassy in Southeast Asia, my question is: why did Slovenia essentially choose the Philippines as its gateway to the region?

That was an important decision. It was a political decision, but also with economic logic. We see the Philippines as a hub, as a central position for us to work with all the countries of ASEAN, which doesn't mean that we are not going to open some other embassies, potentially, but we are making the first step.
So, the Philippines is really important for us from this point of view, and the embassy, as I have seen now, is working really very well.

Yes, Minister. Well, Slovenia, of course, I know, is one of several countries that signed a joint statement in July reaffirming its support for a free and open Indo-Pacific. Of course, this was during the 10th anniversary of the 2016 arbitral ruling. Tell us, what is Slovenia's formal position on this issue?

We are a maritime nation, as you are. So, it is essential, and not only for the Philippines and Slovenia but for all the countries, that we preserve the freedom of navigation, which means, you know, 90% of all the goods, all the trade at the global level, is being done by sea. So, we have to respect international law, and it goes without saying that we Slovenes, we are supporting international institutions, and in this particular case, UNCLOS, that's the Convention on the Law of the Sea, should be respected.

Minister, you mentioned Slovenia, of course, values international law, and I researched Slovenia, and I found out that we do have something in common, in that we have a shared struggle in a border dispute. Of course, the West Philippine Sea is vastly different from Piran Bay, but from your perspective, what support can Slovenia, or if not support, what lessons can Slovenia share with the Philippines when it comes to these kinds of disputes?

I think we have to — and it goes beyond, of course, Slovenia and the Philippines. In this particular case, there are no 100% similarities, but yes, the law of the sea and international law, talking on the general side, should be respected. So, we have to insist on this, but of course, it also goes without saying that we should strive for good neighborhood relations.

So, I am an optimistic person. I served as a diplomat for 30 years and more. Now, I'm a politician, yes, of course, but I think it is always possible if you build a trustworthy relationship with your neighbor, and you will tell me, of course, it's not easy, but in everyday life, it's not easy to build trust.

So, I would see this: of course, the ruling should be respected, if we are talking now about the international arbitration tribunal awards, but also try to find possibilities in this particular case to work with the neighbors. So, I think we have possibilities to communicate, to exchange our, let's say, experience, and basically to work together.

Minister, I like what you said about how we have to strive to build a good and peaceful neighborhood, and on the topic of regional security, do you see a link between Russia's war in Ukraine and security in the South China Sea?

Nowadays, we see what is happening. In a metaphor, I say it is like — we could name it — a thunderstorm, which is kind of embracing the whole planet, more or less, because it's a geopolitical situation, and any crisis or war... You have mentioned the war in Ukraine; that is an aggressive war in Ukraine. And we have to be honest and say that a permanent member of the Security Council of the United Nations, which is supposed to be the main guarantor of peace, is attacking its neighbor, and that definitely is a clear violation of international law.

So, in this case, of course, if the international community would allow one country, a strong country in this particular case, basically to change the borders, or I would say to violate international law with force, that would be kind of undermining the trust around the whole, I would say, environment, even including the South China Sea. Then somebody would say, "Okay, it was possible to do it there, why not here?"

That's why I think we need to work together. We need to have more avenues of communication open, and I strongly believe in the rational kind of judgment that we are here together, we are all interdependent. And if this is going to kind of be prolonged, this war of aggression, it's going to influence the deterioration of the situation here.

I think all those wars are interconnected, and we can see this, and the only solution here is to work together at the international level, and I think the United Nations is the best instrument we have. We don't have anything else at this moment. So, I'm trying to keep the optimism, but the times are really, really demanding.

Well, stepping away from the global maritime arena, I'd like to ask you, Minister, about your visit yesterday or earlier to the school in Bulacan owned by a Slovenian-Filipino couple, can you tell us what your impression of the school was?

I would say I was really impressed. I met all the pupils, the children, then of course the headmaster, and also the couple you mentioned, who are basically the founders of the school. And I think we had this really — because, you know, I always say everything starts and ends with people, and children, they are our future. So, to work with children, to open their, let's say, kind of areas of curiosity, of how important it is that we try to understand interculturally that we are different, but at the end of the day, that we should work together, we should establish friendly relations. And we were also touching upon this really important thing, and that is that this planet wouldn't exist without the pollinators, namely the bees.
I think it was really an extraordinary event, and, you know, when I'm sitting with the children, my heart is melting down.
On the general arena, in terms of main priorities in the Philippines, what would you say is the priority area of cooperation between Slovenia and the Philippines?

Well, we are looking now into — well, at the end of the day, we have to be realistic. In our trade exchange, overall economic exchange, we should benefit both sides, so as to create more prosperity. So now I also had a talk with the business community, with some companies, with the European representative of the European Chamber of Commerce, and I think they are really — the Philippines is developing. We are also benefiting from really high-level skilled Filipino labor. I mean, people are coming to work in Slovenia — we have a few thousand of them already — and I think it's kind of a two-way road.

I hope, and we will be working on this, that the trade is going to deepen, so that we will have even more, hopefully some investments in some areas, for example, water purification, also in some other technological areas. So I think there are good prospects to have our cooperation even on a bigger scale.

Minister, the Philippines is a country of migrant workers, and Slovenia is among the EU members that have called for a stricter migration policy. How, if at all, will this affect Filipinos currently working or aspiring to work in Slovenia?

No, I think hard-working, skilled and rule-abiding people are always welcome, anywhere they go. Here we are talking about illegal migration, which is a huge challenge for Europe and elsewhere. What was said is that Slovenia is for stricter control of the borders — that is, the external borders of the European Union, because internally we have no borders. We have the Schengen regime.
So for workers from the Philippines, nothing will change. I hope they will get higher salaries if we increase our productivity, so that we all benefit from it.
Do you see more job opportunities for Filipinos interested in working in Slovenia?

I think so. There are certain sectors, like health care. Slovenia also has quite a strong industrial production sector. Look also at skills in IT, artificial intelligence and software. I think there will be more job opportunities.
But what I would wish — while of course I respect everyone's wish to travel and work in foreign countries — is for there to be even more job opportunities here in this beautiful country.

My last question, Minister. One very big event Filipinos are awaiting — not here, but in The Hague — is the upcoming International Criminal Court trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte. I mention this because Slovenia recently lifted its entry ban on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. How exactly does Slovenia see its responsibilities as a member of the International Criminal Court?

Thank you for this question. I attended the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in September, and my prime minister — my boss — gave a speech touching on this very issue: international law and our attention to all the open conflicts and crises. You know that, since the Second World War, we are now in a situation with a high number of open conflicts and acts of aggression.

He said — and I think we should all agree with this — that we should treat all of these unselectively, so that we have the same approach to all these conflicts and also to the proceedings being conducted by international bodies.

You asked about Israel. It's a particular issue because it is linked to the situation in Palestine. It goes really far back, but the latest development in the last few years was the really cruel and barbaric attack by the terrorist group Hamas on Israel, and then, of course, what I would call the retaliation, where Israel was protecting itself. This is now being processed, in a way, by the international bodies. I think we should wait until the end. All the evidence, everything, should be brought before justice unselectively, and then I think we should respect the ruling. But let's see what this situation will bring.

For Slovenia, it is important that we stick to international law. This is crucial at this moment in history, which is not easy for any of us. Because if we go back to rules set by those who are militarily stronger, then I think this world will not be more peaceful but rather the opposite, in even more trouble.
Minister, a very last question. What are you hopeful for in terms of Philippine-Slovenian relations?

I'm going to meet Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro now, and I will invite her to come to Slovenia next year. You are also most welcome to come, of course. We will be hosting the 22nd edition of the Bled Strategic Forum. It's a regional think-tank and geopolitical forum, and I hope next year we will also have a roundtable, or let's say a panel, addressing the relations between our regions.

Here I will single out a part of Europe, because the whole European Union has 27 members, and we are in Central Europe. This government, in which I serve as foreign minister, is trying to strengthen regional cooperation in Central Europe: Slovenia, Austria, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary, and we would also add Croatia. Then we are quite a strong group.

So I will be working on this, and I will propose to the foreign secretary a panel on the interaction between the Philippines and Central Europe — or eventually a broader composition, so that it would include not only the Philippines but ASEAN as such. I think that would really bring this to people's attention, because certain companies are still not aware that there are possibilities, new avenues open between our two sides.
