articles.title: Car use in London forecast to rise by 10% in next decade
articles.summary:
Modelling in draft of 10-year London plan threatens Sadiq Khan’s promises on improving air quality

Car use in London will rise by 10% over the next decade with cycling and walking falling as…

blocks.text: Car use in London will rise by 10% over the next decade with cycling and walking falling as a proportion of trips, according to an official forecast by the city’s mayoralty, putting into doubt Sadiq Khan’s promises on air quality and the environment.

Based on projections in the draft version of the latest 10-year London plan, drawn up by the mayor’s office and Transport for London (TfL), road congestion from a growing population would slow buses down, while packed tube services might require stations to close regularly to ease numbers.

Khan’s office said the figures were not a prediction but modelling, based on an assumption of no new transport policies, and did not take into account the impact of recent changes such as the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street.
The expectation was that active travel levels would increase and car use would fall, they added.

The draft plan for 2026-36 sets out three possible models of growth in population and jobs, and thus demand for transport, housing and other services. The central one of these, seen as the most likely, forecasts a population of 9.9 million people, up from the current 9.1 million.
If this happens, according to the plan, the number of car or other motor vehicle trips would rise by 10% between a baseline date of 2023 and 2036, with trips using public transport going up by 17%.
Journeys by active travel, such as walking and cycling, would rise by 6%, resulting in a slight fall as a proportion of all trips taken.

A relative decline in active travel would put London at odds with the trajectory of many other European cities, for example Paris, where bike use almost tripled as a proportion of all trips in just five years.

Mayoral officials, however, dispute that this will actually happen, pointing to London’s recent growth in cycling and walking trips, with new cycle lanes and hundreds of school streets that restrict motor traffic at drop-off and pickup times.
An increase in car journeys would also bring what the report called “significant challenges” on the roads, including a possible 7% reduction in average speeds, slowing down bus routes.

blocks.caption: The London mayor’s office said the modelling did not take into account the recent pedestrianisation of Oxford Street. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: On public transport, overcrowding would become more common, while on the underground, severe overcrowding at some stations “indicates the possible regular need for intervention during periods of peak demand, such as closing stations to entering passengers or nonstopping trains”, it warned.
The modelling calls into question Khan’s progress on greening London’s transport network, given his pledge in 2022 for a 27% reduction in car use across London by 2030.

Ralph Smyth, a strategy adviser for the Transport Action Network campaign group, who uncovered the projections in the plan, said progress on shifting the capital away from car use appeared to have stalled.

He said: “The new London Plan was the opportunity for the mayor to leave a legacy of a cleaner, healthier and less congested city. Inexplicably, he seems to want to turn back the clock and increase cars across the capital.”
after newsletter promotion

Khan has made progress in cleaning up London’s air, particularly with the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone to central and inner London in 2023, but the capital lags behind some other European cities and a shift towards more driving would further stall progress, even with the adoption of electric vehicles.

blocks.caption: Khan has made progress in cleaning up London’s air, particularly with the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone, but the capital still lags behind some other European cities. Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty

blocks.text: The transition to EVs will help, said Jenny Bates, a campaigner from Friends of the Earth, “but this will take many years – and it won’t reduce congestion”.
“London, like many cities, needs to reduce car use and reclaim space for safer walking and cycling routes, and more urban greenery to help cool the city during increasingly hot summers,” she said.
Simon Munk, the head of campaigns for the London Cycling Campaign, said the plan risked “modelling a future that is already out of date”.
He said: “TfL should not be modelling for ongoing heavy car use in London, but instead articulating how to do land-use planning and transport policy to get a lot less of it.”
A spokesperson for the mayor said: “City hall expects active travel will increase significantly by 2036 and car use will fall.

“The modelling in the London plan is based on a scenario in which no additional active travel schemes will be introduced over the next decade – which clearly is not the case, and the modelling will help identify what future transport schemes may be needed.”

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still…

image.caption: Anthropic is aiming for a valuation of more than $1 trillion when it goes public next weekImage: Carlos Barria/REUTERS

blocks.text: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, is set to make its Nasdaq debut Thursday in one of the largest share sales in history.
The Claude maker is offering 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share, which would value it at around $1.3 trillion.
This public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly.
2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.
In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters
AI doubts trigger market turbulence
The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.
While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.
Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.
The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.
In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.
The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

blocks.caption: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is under scrutiny over an affair with an alleged Chinese spyImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO

While OpenAI — the maker of ChatGPT — has delayed its public listing until next year, some analysts have been left scratching their heads at Anthropic's decision to proceed, even though the IPO is reportedly about six times oversubscribed.
"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.
Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."
Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."
Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath
Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive
Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.
In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."
AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction."
"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
Signs to watch, not reasons to flee

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.
"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."
That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.
Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.
Why US voters are fighting Trump's AI data center boom
Is AI next in a long line of bubbles that burst?

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.
Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.
"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.
Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18 to reflect the latest developments.

articles.title: ASEAN energy solutions must go beyond oil — experts
articles.summary: The calls follow Japan's proposal of an oil stockpiling program to insulate the region against global supply shocks.

blocks.text: Climate and Environment
November 19, 2026 | 1:54pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. shakes hands with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday, November 16, the second day of the 49th ASEAN Summit.
Takaichi Sanae via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ long-term fuel and power strategy must focus on accelerating the transition to renewable energy, economics and energy experts said.

The calls follow the launch of various energy security partnerships at the 49th ASEAN Summit, among which was a Japan-backed oil stockpiling proposal announced by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at the Asia Zero Emission Community Summit on Tuesday, November 17.
The offer would make use of Japan’s idle oil tanks and allow participating countries to use the spare storage capacity to secure oil supplies ahead of global supply shocks.

The Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore have agreed to participate in the initiative, with the United Arab Emirates also showing interest. The Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia and the Indonesian Business Council also signed letters of intent with energy companies to explore emergency oil access for the Philippines through existing storage facilities in Indonesia and Thailand.

Takaichi also proposed the creation of an Asia Oil Security Task Force to coordinate oil procurement, stockpiling and emergency releases during major supply disruptions, not unlike the France-based International Energy Agency.

Tim Buckley, director at Climate Energy Finance, called the proposal “farcical,” saying it was like advocate "advocating to adopt last century solutions to the energy security and cost of living crises" linked to conflict in the Middle East.
Buckley argued that China’s response to cutting domestic oil demand through electrification and rapid adoption of wind and solar energy infrastructure was more relevant to the region.
EnergyLab Southeast Asia Regional Co-Director Natharoun Ngo Son likewise said that an Asian energy cooperative should focus on “clean energy, clean electrification and resilience.”

The cooperative, Ngo Son added, should invest in accelerating grid-connection efforts and support organizations to mobilize the resources needed to overcome barriers to the implementation of cross-border power interconnection like the ASEAN Power Grid.
The grid seeks to link national electricity networks in the region by 2040. Member nations signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding on the initiative Sunday.
ASEAN has also expanded energy cooperation with Australia, South Korea and China, covering renewable energy, cross-border electricity trade, energy security and emerging technologies.

Though oil stockpiling is an important and necessary response to the region’s immediate needs, energy security must be built on sustainable and resilient systems for the future, Ser Percival Peña Reyes, senior research fellow at the Ateneo Center for Economic Research and Development said.
Data from the International Energy Agency shows that the Philippines is largely powered by fossil fuels, with coal and oil making up 35% and 29.2% of the country’s energy supply in 2024.
Liquefied natural gas, meanwhile, represents 4.3% of the energy mix.

articles.title: VP Sara's team shows Duterte, Santiago, Corona clips; relevance questioned
articles.summary: The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday presented video clips of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the late senator Miriam Defensor-Santiago, and the late Chief Justice Renato…

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 1:46pm

The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday presented video clips of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the late senator Miriam Defensor-Santiago, and the late Chief Justice Renato Corona, prompting some senator-judges to question the relevance of the materials.

On Day 44 of the impeachment trial, defense counsel Mark Vinluan initially presented a clip of Defensor-Santiago during Corona’s impeachment trial, when she was questioning the withdrawal of articles of impeachment of then-House prosecutors.
What went before: The dropping of impeachment articles against CJ Corona

“What is the relevance of all this, Mr. Presiding Officer?... We’re like watching a movie. Then another thing, pagpahingahin na natin 'yung namayapa. That is a different case, this is a different case. This is a different set of senators. Iba 'yun 'yung sinaunang panahon. I really do not understand why we are watching this,” Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo said.
Senator-judge Panfilo Lacson also said that he did not see the relevance of the clip, as this was the opinion of one of the senator-judges in the 2011 trial.
Senate impeachment presiding officer Francis Escudero agreed with Tulfo, ending the presentation of the clip and telling Vinluan to move on.
Vinluan then asked AML Consulting PH head Rainer Dela Fuente on the effect of withdrawing the charges for the predicate crime when it comes to investigating money laundering activities.
House prosecutor and Akbayan Rep. Chel Diokno objected to the question.

Vinluan also presented a clip of Corona being emotional when he faced the impeachment court and saying that it was being used to persecute him. Diokno again questioned the clip, saying that it was irrelevant.

“I do not see the relevance of the statements made by the Chief Justice Corona about his alleged persecution, except that it is an appeal to emotion that I believe has no place in this impeachment trial. Whatever question asked would be immaterial, it would be irrelevant because we could not even cross-examine the late Chief Justice Corona on his statements. And it would be misleading because there is no such evidence of persecution in this case before the court,” Diokno said.
But Vinluan said that impeachment was not a purely legal proceeding.

“There’s a political aspect to it. And I think, your Honor, we’ve been prudent in laying the foundation for our questions so again, Your Honor, we just ask for a little leeway for the defense. The prosecution has had its time,” he said.
After the video was finished, Vinluan asked Dela Fuente on the effect of weaponizing the AMLC against an individual.

“Under Section 16 of the AMLA, Your Honor, there is a prohibition on the use of AMLC information for political persecution. Aside from political persecution, to hamper commerce and trade,” Dela Fuente said.

Lastly, the defense presented a clip of the Vice President’s father, Rodrigo Duterte, when he was asked about a possible impeachment case against then vice president Leni Robredo. Duterte said that he disagreed with any impeachment cases against Robredo.

Vinluan asked Dela Fuente if it was possible for data from the AMLC to be used for prosecution in an impeachment proceeding. Diokno questioned this again, saying that Dela Fuente was a financial investigator for only two years.
Dela Fuente was allowed to answer, merely saying it was possible for AMLC data to be used in such a way.

Before the impeachment court called for a recess, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros made a manifestation raising a concern on the clips presented. She said that Corona and Defensor-Santiago have both passed, and Rodrigo Duterte is not in the Philippines.
None of them could be questioned by the senator-judges, Hontiveros said.
“Hindi po fair 'yung ganitong situation. Hindi po fair, either sa tatlong taong pinakita 'yung video nila, hindi rin po fair sa Senate impeachment court na ito,” she said.
(This situation is not fair. It is not fair, either to the three people whose videos were shown, and it is not fair for this Senate impeachment court.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Remarkable luck’: wreck of first Australian-built warship discovered exactly 128 years after sinking
articles.summary:
HMCS Spitfire commissioned by colonial government to protect against Russian warships based at Vladivostok during Crimean war

The wreck of Australia’s first locally-built warship has been…

blocks.text: The wreck of Australia’s first locally built warship has been discovered 128 years after sinking off the coast of far north Queensland.
Marine archaeologists found the remains of Ex HMCS Spitfire on 21 August, the anniversary of its sinking in 1898.

Celeste Jordan, the principal heritage officer at Queensland’s Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation, said it was “remarkable luck”. Rediscovering lost shipwrecks would “help ensure the stories of our past are preserved, celebrated and protected for future generations”, she said.

The 19-metre wooden gunboat, designed and built in Sydney in 1855, was commissioned by the Australian colonial government to protect against Russian warships based at Vladivostok during the Crimean war and amid concern about the French military presence in New Caledonia. It was designed to carry a 32-pounder cannon, although evidence suggests the armament may never have been fitted.

blocks.caption: The wreck of the former HMCS Spitfire, which was discovered by divers.  Photograph: Jay Cronan/Department of Defence

blocks.text: The clipper later served Queensland as a pilot vessel, before it was sold for £300 into private hands as a sea cucumber fishing vessel.

A 1981 article in the Naval Historical Review described the boat as “a sturdy little vessel”. Constructed from ironbark and blackwood, and sheathed in copper, it was designed and built by the Sydney shipbuilder John Cuthbert, and launched by his wife Susan Cuthbert from Darling Harbour in 1855.

On 21 August 1898, Spitfire developed a leak and foundered on a voyage off the coast of Queensland’s Cape York peninsula, according to the Australian National Maritime Museum. Its crew were rescued by the Japanese steamship Omi Maru.

A crew from the Australian National Maritime Museum, Queensland government and the Royal Australian Navy, found the wreck while aboard HMAS Diamantina, a minehunter vessel. The month-long expedition searched an area based on archival records, with sonar picking up the Spitfire as an acoustic anomaly.

The Chief of Navy, Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley, said the Spitfire occupied a unique place in Australia’s naval history. “For sailors today, this vessel represents the beginning of a story that continues in the Royal Australian Navy.”
The wreck is protected under the Underwater Cultural Heritage Act 2018, and is one of more than 8,000 shipwrecks, sunken aircraft and other heritage sites in Australian waters.

articles.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
articles.summary:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four…

blocks.text: The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

blocks.caption: A datacentre under construction at the Google Storey County campus in Sparks, Nevada, US. Photograph: Daniel Cole/Reuters

blocks.text: Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

blocks.caption: Workers at TikTok’s datacentre in Hamar, Norway. Photograph: Victoria Klesty/Reuters

blocks.text: The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

articles.title: Hannah Lillith Assadi wins National book award for ‘visionary’ novel Paradiso 17
articles.summary:
Assadi’s third novel was inspired by the story of her late father, a Palestinian who escaped the Nakba as a child in 1948

Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National…

blocks.text: Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.

Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba in 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel. The story was inspired by her father, Sami Abdul-Fattah Al-Assadi, who fled the Nakba as a child with his family, before studying in Italy and moving to New York.
In a tearful speech, Assadi said, “What a beautiful story this has been, from its origins at my father’s deathbed until now, ending here and accepting this award. And so full of pain.

“In the course of its writing, I have experienced deep personal grief and unimaginable collective grief. I have watched cancer ravage my father’s body and genocide ravage his people and their children. And perhaps this is the Palestinian story on this earth. So beautiful. So painful.”
The judges praised Assadi’s “elegant lyricism” and “ambitious bending of time and space” and called the novel “a visionary, finely wrought portrait of rupture and endurance”.
Assadi won the $10,000 prize against Edwidge Danticat’s Dèy, Julián Delgado Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You, Valeria Luiselli’s Beginning Middle End and Morgan Thomas’ Mad Eden.

Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy won the $10,000 nonfiction prize for his debut Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, about his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt. ElGendy was unable to attend the ceremony after being denied a visa to the US, so his prize was collected by his editor Helen Thomaides, who read out his speech.

ElGendy said he had dreamed of turning his experience into a memoir as it gave him distance from the physical abuse he endured, and revealed he had practised award acceptance speeches under his duvet in prison.

“Today that dream should have come full circle but, like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable,” ElGendy wrote.

The New York Times speculated earlier this month that ElGendy was not even eligible for the award as he did not meet its citizenship or residency requirements after fleeing the US due to Ice deportations, but the National Book Foundation, which administers the National book Awards, disputed this and said it did not “have any concerns regarding the eligibility of his title”.
Samar Yazbek of Syria, a finalist for the books in translation category, was also denied a visa, with the National Book Foundation describing both decisions as “unjust”.

The state department declined to comment on any specific cases, but issued a statement to Associated Press saying that “the Trump Administration continues to put America and its interests first by fully enforcing US immigration laws and ensuring lawful travel through our visa process. As Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio said, ‘a visa is a privilege, not a right’.”

blocks.caption: Salman Rushdie on the red carpet before the ceremony, where he was awarded a medal for lifetime achievement. Photograph: John Lamparski/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Publishers submitted 1,912 books to the National book awards this year, with the winners judged by panels of authors, editors, booksellers and others in the literary community.

Brenda Hillman won the $10,000 poetry category for Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation, praised as “a rigorously unsentimental portrait of the stillness … of the poet’s childhood home after her mother’s death”.
David Leviathan and Gabriel Duckels won the $10,000 young people’s literature category for The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America.

Indian-British author Salman Rushdie was presented with a medal for “distinguished contribution to American letters”, while paediatrician and author Perri Klass was honoured for “outstanding service to the American literary community”.

Rushdie recalled being welcomed into the US literary scene after spending years under police protection in London after the fatwa over The Satanic Verses, and used his speech to thank the late Ursula K Le Guin for liking his first novel. “She was just about the only one who did! And it meant everything to me,” he said, to laughs.
“All I want to say is that it has been quite a ride, from over there to over here,” he added. “And to ride into this town and end up in this saloon, with these companions, is a hell of a thing.”
Actor and author Kyle MacLachlan hosted the ceremony, held at Cipriani Wall Street, while singer Michelle Zauner, author of the bestselling memoir Crying in H Mart, performed onstage.

blocks.text: The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division declared three co-accused of former lawmaker Zaldy Co as "fugitives" from justice in connection to graft charges.
In a six-page resolution promulgated on November 10, the anti-graft court also ordered the cancellation of passports of Timojen Sacar, Anthony Ngo, and Consuelo Aldon.
The ruling noted that the three individuals remained at large amid the arrest warrants and hold departure order issued against them on November 21, 2025.

"Given the high-profile nature of the case, it is reasonable to conclude that the accused are aware of the criminal proceedings and the outstanding warrants issued against them," the ruling penned by Associate Justice Zaldy Trespeses read.

"Thus, by stating beyond the reach of law enforcement while fully aware of pending warrants of arrest confirms accused's deliberate intent to evade judicial process. By choosing to remain at large for nearly a year, accused Sacar, Ngo, and Aldon have rendered themselves fugitives from justice," it added.
The anti-graft court also said that the cancellation of their passports "hinders attempts to evade judicial processes."

"The cancellation of fugitive's passport is an essential remedy to address the flight risk posed by individuals facing criminal charges, thereby safeguarding the administration of criminal justice," it ruled.
Co and the three fugitives are facing graft charges linked to alleged anomalies in flood-control and infrastructure projects.
The former Ako Bicol partylist representative also remains at large, though it was previously reported that he could be in Europe.

articles.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
articles.summary: The meeting comes with challenges as there are things Xi does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit
ByLaura Bicker
China correspondent Reporting fromShenzhen
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fourth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fourth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives

blocks.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fourth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives

The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.
China's growing nuclear arsenal
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025

blocks.text: China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.
Will everyone stick to the script?
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.
Xi's problems at home
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy

blocks.text: A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

articles.title: NUPL says 7 minors from ASEAN protest still in custody; LGU says discharge process ongoing
articles.summary: Seven minors apprehended in connection with a protest action during the November 15 opening of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit remain in custody as of Thursday morning,…

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 12:37pm

Seven minors apprehended in connection with a protest action during the November 15 opening of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit remain in custody as of Thursday morning, the National Union of Peoples' Lawyers (NUPL) said.

The NUPL disputed the Department of Justice's (DOJ) November 18 announcement that all 20 minors arrested in connection with the Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan protest caravan had already been released.
"As of this writing, seven (7) minors remain in custody and are still undergoing discharge conferences. None of these seven (7) minors has been released," the NUPL said in a statement.
The lawyers' group called on the DOJ to immediately correct its statement and accurately disclose the continuing detention of the minors.
Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office ordered the release of the anti-Trump and anti-Pax Silica protesters from detention and custody on Wednesday.

While NUPL welcomed the release of 216 protesters and journalists from Camp Bagong Diwa, along with five other minors from Bahay Pag-asa child care institution, the group called out the alleged delay in the release of seven more minors from Bahay Pag-asa.
Discharge procedures

Muntinlupa Mayor Ruffy Biazon, meanwhile, said Bahay Pag-asa had started the discharge procedures for the minors following the City Prosecutor's resolution ordering their release for further investigation.

He said the minors would be released immediately after completing the procedures, which include exit interviews, inventory of personal belongings, preparation of discharge documents, and conferences with their parents or guardians.

"Bagaman natanggap ng Bahay Pagasa ang resolusyon kahapon ng alas-singko ng hapon, matapos ang konsultasyon sa mga magulang, nagdesisyon ang BP na papahingahin muna ang mga bata at isagawa ng discharge procedure agaran ngayong umaga," he said.

(Although Bahay Pagasa received the resolution yesterday at 5 p.m., after consultation with the parents, BP decided to let the children rest first and conduct the discharge procedure immediately this morning.)
After consulting with the parents, however, the mayor said Bahay Pag-asa decided to let the minors rest before proceeding with their discharge on Thursday.

Biazon explained that Bahay Pag-asa, a facility for children in conflict with the law, follows specific procedures to ensure the minors' well-being, particularly those who may have experienced psychological stress or trauma. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: No terms yet in Trump's 'biggest trade deal' with the Philippines
articles.summary: “Basically, the US market is being opened for us to get good quality agricultural products, things we need for food security that we import anyway,” Romualdez said.

blocks.text: Headlines
November 19, 2026 | 12:28pm
US President Donald Trump (L) and Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr shake hands during a bilateral meeting at Malacanang Palace in Manila on November 18, 2026.
AFP / Rolex Dela Pena / Pool
MANILA, Philippines — The “trade deal” that United States President Donald Trump boasted of yesterday as the biggest ever between Washington and Manila has yet to be turned into a concrete agreement.

Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez said on Thursday, November 19, that the talks produced only a broad offer from Trump for the US to supply the Philippines' food and energy needs, with the terms still to be worked out.

“There are really no details yet. It’s just generalities for now,” Romualdez said in a DZBB interview in mixed English and Filipino. “President Trump offered that our food security and our energy security [needs] could be supplied by the US.”

Trump made the announcement on Wednesday at a state luncheon in Malacañang, the final event of a brief state visit in which President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. hosted the US delegation, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far. And it’s a fair deal for both countries,” Trump said. He added that “it took place very quickly,” but gave no further details.

The two leaders left the meeting without signing any agreement. In a social media post as he flew to China, Trump described “a new and completely different Trade Deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark,” and said it would be great for American farmers and “those in the business of Energy.”

A later statement from the Presidential Communications Office was more tempered in that it said the two countries had “reached an understanding” on key areas of economic cooperation, particularly energy and food security, and that trade representatives “will work closely to translate these commitments into concrete initiatives.”

A fact sheet released by the White House yesterday, in turn, said Trump and Marcos "committed to eliminate the U.S. trade deficit with the Philippines" by increasing "Philippine imports of American energy and agriculture products."

Little has actually been shared about whether Marcos was able to bring up tariffs with Trump, specifically the 12.5% tariff covering about a third of the country's US-bound exports, or roughly $6.25 billion worth of goods.
The US is the Philippines’ biggest export market, taking $2.63 billion, or 26.6%, of its shipments in September, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.

Romualdez said in his interview Thursday that Trump had asked why the Philippines was still buying from other countries when it could buy from the US instead. He noted that the Philippines runs a trade surplus with the US.
“Basically, the US market is being opened for us to get good quality agricultural products, things we need for food security that we import anyway,” Romualdez said.
On energy, he said Trump had opened up US oil for export, citing pipelines being built in Alaska that would bring oil to Asia through Japan.

The Alaska project the Trump administration has promoted to Japan, South Korea and other Asian allies is a proposed 1,300-km pipeline carrying natural gas from the state’s North Slope for export as liquefied natural gas.
Romualdez also addressed Pax Silica, the US-led initiative to build semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains less reliant on China, which the Philippines joined in April.

Reports that a Pax Silica agreement would be signed during Trump’s visit drew week-long protests, as a broad alliance of progressive groups and civil society organizations say such a deal would ravage communities and pollute the environment here.

“No data center is being discussed,” Romualdez said. “We’re not even calling it Pax Silica. It’s more of a development, a manufacturing hub that will have not only US companies but other companies.” He said these included firms from Taiwan and others looking to relocate to the Philippines.

articles.title: General Pants Co enters voluntary administration, putting hundreds of jobs at risk
articles.summary:
Australian fashion chain becomes latest retailer in trouble after David Jones, Cue and Veronika Maine

  • Get our

blocks.text: The youth fashion chain General Pants Co has become the latest major retailer to slide into voluntary administration, putting nearly 500 jobs at risk as Australia’s retail sector continues to struggle with cash-strapped shoppers and online-only competitors.

The collapse comes not long after that of upmarket department store David Jones and premium womenswear brands Cue and Veronika Maine, underscoring the mounting toll of tough economic conditions on established retailers.
The consultancy Alvarez & Marsal confirmed it had taken control of General Pants Co and nine related businesses after being appointed their voluntary administrator late on Wednesday evening.

In a statement, the administrators said they were working closely with the existing management team to undertake an urgent assessment of the business, including its trading performance, stores, stock and costs.

All 35 General Pants Co stores and its online store would remain open and trading as usual while the administrators worked out whether they could sell or restructure the business to keep it afloat, the firm said.

A spokesperson for General Pants Co’s parent company, Alquemie group, said it had progressively cut the number of physical stores due to the “recent Australian retail trading environment, and rapid structural changes in the sector, including the growing dominance of offshore online-only retailers”.

They said they had tried a “range of options” to save General Pants Co from administration, including attempting to sell the business or securing a “significant capital injection” to help it better compete against large scale competitors.
“None were ultimately viable,” they said.
They said the voluntary administration process will examine whether General Pants Co could be restructured into a smaller scale, “more focussed” and, ultimately, viable business.

blocks.caption: General Pants Co is not the only Australian retailer under significant pressure. Photograph: Richard Milnes/Alamy

blocks.text: Alvarez & Marsal said the 500 people employed by General Pants Co across Australia and New Zealand would continue to be paid for the work they did during the administration period.

Additionally, the consultancy said staff entitlements accrued prior to the appointment remained legally protected under the Corporations Act and of a higher priority to administrators than “most” other unsecured creditor claims.
Two of the Alvarez & Marsal managing directors, Jason Tracy and Glen Kanevsky, were appointed to oversee the administration, with a first meeting with creditors due to be held on 30 November.
Tracy described General Pants Co as “one of Australia’s best-known youth fashion brands, with a loyal customer base and a dedicated team”.
He said the administrators’ immediate priorities were to keep the stores trading, support employees and customers, and pursue “a sale and/or recapitalisation” of the business.
“With Black Friday next week, we are focused on maximising trading performance and expect strong demand over the period,” Tracy said.
“We thank the team members, landlords and suppliers of General Pants Co for their support as we work through the administration.”

General Pants Co, which began in 1972 as a specialty denim store on Sydney’s George Street and has traded across Australia and New Zealand since, is not the only Australian retailer under significant pressure.

Last week, the embattled upmarket retailer David Jones entered administration with more than $400m owed to creditors. Less than two months earlier, Cue Clothing Co, the owner of mainstay Australian labels Cue and Veronika Maine, entered administration and receivership in September.
Last year, Mosaic Group, the owner of brands including Noni B, Rivers, and Katies, was liquidated.
While Australian retailers deal with their own increased operating costs, indebted households are tightened their budgets during a new bout of inflationary pressures.
This strain is driving a sharp contraction across the sector, according to credit reporting agency Equifax, marked by surging business closures and a slowdown in new brands.
Equifax’s Brad Walters said that the strain was not limited to large retailers such as David Jones.
“Smaller retailers are also dealing with a difficult combination of softer discretionary spending, rising operating costs and increasingly narrow financial buffers,” Walters said.
“Instead of funding long-term expansion, smaller operators are taking on credit simply to manage immediate overheads.”

While David Jones is closing half of its 38-store network, rival Myer is facing its own financial stress, with the chain forced to offer “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”.
Four out of Myer’s five newly acquired apparel chains – Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti, and Jacqui E – recorded falling sales last financial year, leaving Just Jeans as the sole brand to post growth.

articles.title: ‘Shame old Aussies’ to ‘fresh chaos’: what the UK papers say about Bancroft’s explosive ball tampering claims
articles.summary:
Sports sections of British newspapers deliver their take on the unfolding Cricket Australia sandpaper saga

The sports sections of the UK’s major mastheads are relishing the never-ending…

blocks.text: The sports sections of the UK’s major mastheads are relishing the never-ending crisis engulfing Australian cricketing, after a key player in the ball tampering controversy, Cameron Bancroft, alleged everyone on the team knew about the 2018 plot.

Bancroft’s allegation came five days after a lengthy media conference by the current Australia Test captain, Pat Cummins, during which he denied that everyone on the team was in on the sandpaper plan. Cummins was responding to the allegation first aired in teammate Usman Khawaja’s biography, that actually, everyone did know about the sandpaper Bancroft was later caught holding.

The Guardian wrote “Australia turmoil” before giving readers a full rundown of “who said what” and an op-ed from commentator Geoff Lemon, who wrote Bancroft “delivered a devastating repudiation of Cummins”.

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: The Daily Star’s sport section promised readers “an idiot’s guide to sandpapering a cricket ball”. Its opening paragraphs ran through a quick account of the controversy, which the Star labelled a “CRISIS”.
The tabloid’s final words on the matter? “SHAME OLD AUSSIES: Australian Captain Pat Cummins is deep in the didgeridoo-doo.”
The Mirror ran with the headline: “Bancroft: Whole team knew we were CHEATING”. The tabloid said the allegation had sent Cricket Australia “into an even bigger crisis”.

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Mirror

blocks.text: The unfolding scandal also made it to the front page of The Times’ sports section, where the masthead led with the headline: “Cummins did know of plot, says Bancroft”. Playing a straight bat, the paper ran readers through the unfolding controversy, running down to the denial in 2021 from the four senior bowlers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon – that they did not know there was a “foreign substance” taken on to the field to alter the ball.

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Times

blocks.text: The Daily Telegraph also ran the story on the front of its sports pages, with the headline “Explosive Bancroft claim leaves Cummins in peril” accompanied by a headline for an opinion piece calling for the truth to finally come out.

The paper pointed out that the “dramatic intervention in the sandpaper furore came on the same day that Australia were well beaten by England in Hobart, as the tourists clinched the one-day international series”.

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Daily Telegraph

blocks.text: The Daily Express went with alliteration – “Bancroft Bombshell” – also painting the allegations as sending “Australian cricket into an even bigger crisis”.

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Daily Express

blocks.text: Finally, The Daily Mail headlined with “Aussies plunged into fresh chaos” before giving its rundown.

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Daily Mail

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Cricket Australia is rushing to contain the “crisis”, announcing the creation of an independent “forum” for players and staff to share their accounts of the infamous South Africa tour.

articles.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
articles.summary:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world has no power of consent if their husband or…

blocks.text: One in four women around the world has no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Crimean Bridge attacked for a third time this week
This is the third Ukrainian attack this week targeting the key strategic bridge that is a key symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
The bridge has played a key role in supplying Russian troops in occupied parts of southern Ukraine since the 2022 Russian invasion, making it a key target for Kyiv.

Ukraine's SBU security service had said that the "road span beneath it (the arch) has been completely destroyed."
The latest attack appears to have impacted rail traffic on the bridge, according to German press agency DPA.

articles.title: Philippines eyes over $2-billion US military loan after Trump visit
articles.summary: The same information sheet describes the package as a "historic" deal that would "support over 7,000 American jobs" and advance the US' "first arms transfer strategy, all while protecting returns for…

blocks.text: November 19, 2026 | 11:17am
US President Donald Trump arrives in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for the 49th ASEAN Summit.
Facebook / ASEAN 2026 PH

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is eyeing a loan of more than $2 billion (over P127 billion) from the United States to buy defense and security equipment from American suppliers, plus $400 million (around P25 billion) in military financing for deterrence operations in the South China Sea, the White House announced on Thursday, November 19.
The amounts were listed in a White House information sheet released after US President Donald Trump wrapped up a two-day visit to Manila.

Under the "historic foreign military financing loan package," the Philippine government would be using the loan to procure defense and security equipment from US suppliers that would "provide the Philippines with critical defense and security capabilities," the government release read.

The same information sheet describes the package as a "historic" deal that would "support over 7,000 American jobs" and advance the US' "first arms transfer strategy, all while protecting returns for the American taxpayer."

On top of this, the US is also providing the Philippines $400 million in foreign military financing "to expand its operational reach and deterrence capabilities in the South China Sea." This includes procuring long-range fires, command and control systems, critical infrastructure, and drones, according to the information sheet.
Up to $500 million a year in military financing grants had been previously authorized by the US Congress for the Philippines from 2026 to 2030.

The White House also announced two separate agreements between the Philippines' Department of National Defense (DND) and US firms it did not name, which will provide the DND with artificial intelligence-enabled mission support and defense infrastructure.
The US is the only country with which the Philippines has a mutual defense treaty, which covers armed attacks on either country’s armed forces in the South China Sea, including coast guard ships.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to the treaty as recently as July.

The announcement comes after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said at the close of the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila on Wednesday, November 18, that negotiations for the South China Sea code of conduct, a framework of rules to manage disputes in the area, were “85% to 90%” complete.
Negotiations will continue under Singapore, which takes over the ASEAN chairship in 2027.
Beyond defense, Marcos and Trump had also discussed economic cooperation, including what the US president claimed was Washington's "biggest trade deal" ever.
A later release by the Presidential Communications Office said both sides "have reached an understanding" on energy and food security.

articles.title: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
articles.summary: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.

blocks.text: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the campaign's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the Senate and House, while Texas, Ohio and other states swung away from Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living.
Musk was speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Democrats have vowed greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the roll out of controversial data centres.

articles.title: Elon Musk claims ‘I’m not Maga’ and says he regrets vast sums to back Republicans
articles.summary:
Musk, who aligned with Trump and was frequent White House guest, says he feels ‘pretty foolish’ about record midterm spending

Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning…

blocks.text: Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since 2024.

“I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia.

“I’m not sure what Maga means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that,” the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla added.
Musk famously declared at a 2024 campaign rally in Madison Square Garden: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”

In a 45-minute interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin, a New York Times columnist, Musk also said it would be good for Washington to have split control between the two parties, and that he thinks “there are positives and negatives in both”.

He also accused Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of “lying” about restrictions on access to his firm’s Starshield satellite system; praised Jensen Huang, the ousted Nvidia chief executive; and said that “no one I met at Anthropic set off my evil detector”.

Asked about his previous negative comments about Anthropic, Musk said that before he agreed to rent computing power to the AI firm: “I went to met with a lot of people at Anthropic. I didn’t just move forward with the deal.”
“My interaction so far with the Anthropic team is that they seem like good people and they seem principled,” Musk added. “They seem diligent and they seem seem to care about the future.”
Musk donated at least $250m of his own money to help Trump win the election in 2024, and recently spent nearly $500m in the US midterms to support Republicans, many of whom lost.

Musk admitted at the Dealbook summit that his spending had “failed”, and that he felt “pretty foolish” for spending such a sum, the most that anyone has ever spent in a political cycle when they themselves did not run for office. “It certainly shows that American elections are not just about money,” he said. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

After Trump took office for the second time in 2025, Musk served for 180 days heading the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) within Trump’s administration, before stepping down following a very public falling out with the president.

That culminated in Musk posting on his social media platform in June of that year: “Time to drop the really big bomb: @realDonaldTrump is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public.”

The two men later reconciled. During his time leading Doge, Musk frequently appeared in the Oval Office and at cabinet meetings alongside the president, often sporting hats that read “Make America Great Again” or “Trump was right about everything”.

articles.title: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
articles.summary: The head of Crimea said traffic was suspended after another attack on the link between Russia and the occupied territory.

blocks.text: Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.

At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

articles.title: Record-breaking rain lashes California’s Bay area as ‘atmospheric river’ arrives
articles.summary:
Storm expected to move into southern California, with LA residents warned of potential evacuation orders

Heavy rain pounded California’s Bay area, with record rainfall in downtown San…

blocks.text: Heavy rain pounded California’s Bay area, with record rainfall in downtown San Francisco and flooding and power outages across the region, as an “atmospheric river” arrived on Wednesday and dumped precipitation across the state.

The storm was expected to move into southern California on Wednesday night and Thursday, with Los Angeles warning residents in mudslide-prone areas of potential evacuation orders to come. Southern Californians were also warned of potential coastal flooding, heavy surf, wave damage to coastal piers and parking lots and beach sand erosion. Heavy snow warnings were issued for higher elevations of the Sierra Mountains, including in the Greater Lake Tahoe area.

Downtown San Francisco saw the most rainfall before noon in 76 years, at 2.11in, surpassing a record from 1950, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. By 3pm, Wednesday’s daily total of 2.28in had broken the record for the most rainfall on 18 November, which was previously set in 1918, the National Weather Service reported. South of San Francisco, in Santa Clara, there was flooding and standing water on several highways.

In San Jose, the local fire department posted on social media that two vehicles with passengers inside had become stranded in the flooded streets downtown near the SAP Center, the city’s major events arena. The second passenger was being extricated via a boat rescue, the department wrote.
Daniel Lurie, the San Francisco mayor, warned city residents the region’s winter storm and flood season, supercharged by this year’s very strong El Niño weather, was just getting started.

blocks.caption: Crews working at the flooded area on Alemany Blvd at the entrance of Highway 101 in San Francisco, California. Photograph: Tayfun Coşkun/Anadolu / Getty Images

blocks.text: Despite the Wednesday afternoon break in the rain, he posted on social media, “The storm should pick back up tonight, and more rain is in the forecast for next week.”
“When these heavy storms come, we expect flooding to return to many of the same areas that were impacted this morning,” he added.
“Today’s storm certainly gave the Bay Area a good assessment of our pain points for future storms this season,” Drew Tuma, a local meteorologist for ABC7 News, wrote on social media.

Street flooding in San Francisco left maintenance hole covers floating in one neighborhood of San Francisco, while the self-driving car company Waymo temporarily suspended service in the city, the Chronicle reported. One Waymo stalled in a flooded street and blocked traffic, ABC7 News reported.

An overwhelmed sewer stormwater system also appeared to result in several “sewage geysers”, one reportedly 15-ft tall, the Chronicle reported, sharing bystander footage of the spew in the city’s Ocean Beach neighborhood.

Thousands across the Bay area were dealing with storm-related power outages by Wednesday afternoon, according to a customer outage map from Pacific Gas & Electric, the major utility company for much of northern California.

In Monterey, south of San Francisco, the local aquarium posted on social media that “storms and massive waves are causing a surge of sea otter strandings this week in Monterey Bay” and that their staff “safely rescued several pups” after receiving calls from local community members.

blocks.caption: A car in flood water near Highway 101 in Sausalito, California.  Photograph: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

blocks.text: Areas of the state still recovering from recent wildfires continue to be at risk for flash flooding, with specific warnings issued for “burn scar” areas including in Big Sur and the Napa valley.

In Los Angeles, city officials warned residents of areas burned by the 2025 Palisades, Sunset and Hurst fires, north of the city, to be prepared for potential evacuation orders starting on Wednesday night, as heavy rains brought increased risk of flooding, mudslide and debris flow.

Statewide, the heaviest of the rainfall was expected north-east of San Francisco, from Santa Rosa to Chico and Redding in the state’s Central valley, and in the southern part of the Bay Area, along coastal mountain ranges from Santa Cruz to San Jose and Palo Alto, according to the National Weather Service.
“Travel delays, localized flooding and hazardous conditions are possible, especially along the coast and on mountain pass roads,” AccuWeather warned in an online forecast.

Atmospheric rivers, massive currents of water vapor that can carry as much or even more water than an actual river, have been growing stronger and deadlier in recent years. In the relatively dry western US, atmospheric river storms provide both essential precipitation and flood risk.

In southern California, the NWS predicted 1-3in of rain in many areas, with 3in-5in in some mountain and foothill areas, and a 20% chance of thunderstorms on Wednesday and Thursday. As much as a foot of snow was expected in higher-elevation areas above 6,000ft. There was a high risk of “significant road flooding” and a moderate risk for rockslides and mudslides, the NWS said.

The risk of coastal wave damage was expected to peak in southern California on Thursday, with additional risks expected next week, with seasonal high tides overlapping with storm risks during Thanksgiving week.
Waterspouts were spotted over the San Francisco Bay earlier this week, and the NWS flagged the risk of additional waterspouts over the ocean east of San Francisco on Wednesday.
