articles.title: First Nations health watchdog investigating how Sask. boy lost use of small intestine after routine surgery
articles.summary: Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.

image.caption: First Nations Health Ombudsperson Dianne Lafond, right, and Kristen Lerat, centre, speak to media in Saskatoon on Wednesday. (Chanss Lagaden/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New
Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.
Sask. Health Authority also conducting internal review
Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost the use of his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.
Sheldon OneBear Rosebluff, 4, is now in critical condition at the Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon. He requires a small intestine transplant.
On Wednesday, his family and First Nations leaders held a media event to discuss the case and ongoing concerns about how Indigenous people are treated by the provincial health-care system.

First Nations Health Ombudsperson Dianne Lafond said she launched an investigation into Rosebluff's medical ordeal after the boy's family filed a complaint. Lafond said she can't discuss the details of Rosebluff's situation until the investigation is complete.

"Nothing is black and white and some cases are very complex," Lafond said on Wednesday. "When a child goes in for a simple procedure and will now be in the health-care system for years … you've got a lot of different factors at play."
The Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) confirmed it is conducting its own review of the care Rosebluff received in hospital.

items: FSIN appoints ombudsperson to investigate racism in health care

blocks.text: Kristin Lerat is Rosebluff's biological aunt and has been his caregiver for about three years. She described Rosebluff as a talkative boy who likes to build forts, dance and drum.
"A happy, energized boy. And this has taken the richness out of not only his life, but our lives too," Lerat said.
In September, Rosebluff had a successful surgery in Regina for appendicitis. He appeared to be recovering well until Oct. 24, when he suddenly turned ill and was taken back to hospital, Lerat said.

He had a blockage in his bowels and required surgery. After two surgeries in Regina within days, he was airlifted to Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon, where he eventually had two more surgeries over the course of a week.
"He was critical the whole time, but his body just couldn't handle that many surgeries," Lerat said.
Something happened that "killed" his small intestine and he now requires a transplant, Lerat said.
Sheldon One Bear Rosebluff, 4, seen here in an undated photo prior to his medical ordeal. (Submitted by Kristen Lerat)
The SHA declined to comment on Rosebluff surgeries and his condition due to privacy legislation.
But the SHA is conducting a review of the care Rosebluff received and "what might have occured," according to a statement emailed to CBC.

"Patient safety and the delivery of high-quality, patient-centred care remain top priorities for the SHA, and we take patient safety concerns very seriously," SHA chief medical officer Dr. Rashaad Hansia said in the statement.

"Social Work supports are in place to assist in liaising with the family and coordinating with partner agencies, and we are commit[ted] to ensuring these interactions and supports are provided in a culturally respectful way."
Lafond did not provided a timeline for the ombudsperson investigation, but said more details will be released once it is complete.
Cowessess First Nation Chief Erica Beaudin attended the media event to support the Lerat family.
"We are not here to denounce the health-care system or the people in it," Beaudin said.
"What we're talking about is how we must recognize when we must do better.… For us, treaty is not a land acknowledgement. It is action."
The First Nations Health Ombudsperson is an independent office established by the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations to investigate complaints about the health-care system.

In October 2025, the ombudsperson said her office had received about 500 complaints since opening in 2023. About 64 per cent of the cases derived from complaints and issues associated with the services of the Saskatchewan Health Authority.

The boy's family is also concerned about being sidelined for important medical decisions. Lerat said the social services ministry took over decision-making for Rosebluff's care once the boy's condition turned critical.

"It was me and the doctors making the decisions. Now it's the ministries and the doctors making decisions," Lerat said. "So if we get a doctor that does not believe in our traditional ways, what does that look like?"
The Ministry of Social Services provided a statement to CBC.
"Due to provisions in The Child and Family Services Act, the Ministry of Social Services is unable to confirm involvement with a family or speak to specific details of any case," it said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeremy Warren is a reporter in Saskatoon. You can reach him at jeremy.warren@cbc.ca.

articles.title: EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences
articles.summary:
Von der Leyen says she wants to give Kyiv ‘strong hand’ in talks and is confident all 27 member states will back idea

The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to…

blocks.text: The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to help with a looming cash crisis and reinforce its defences, as Russia’s relentless bombardment continues.

Announcing the plan to lend Kyiv the money in 2027, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table. And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”
She expressed confidence all 27 member states would stand behind the loan, despite four central and eastern European countries having already ruled themselves out.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he hoped for the swift adoption of the loan and was counting on the support of all EU member states: “Strong support for Ukraine is the best signal to Russia that this war must end,” he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy convinced EU leaders last month that his country faced a €70bn funding gap in 2027. The EU pledged to cover €45bn and wants Ukraine’s other allies to cover the rest.

Only 11 months ago, the EU agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, which was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s military and civilian needs in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia’s attacks have escalated, the cost of Ukraine’s defence and the toll of economic disruption continue to rise.

Andrius Kubilius, the EU defence commissioner, said Ukraine’s military spending was increasingly dominated by drones. Ukraine, he told reporters, expected Russia to use 10m drones this year and 20m in 2027. “Ukraine with EU assistance needs to match – and will match,” he said.
The EU loan is split into two parts: €25bn for weapons and €20bn for civilian needs, including funding essential services, such as schools and hospitals.

Von der Leyen expressed confidence that all member states would support the loan because “all 27 member states say very clearly that they want to support Ukraine”. She said member states could choose to support Ukraine’s civilian needs, rather than military spending.

Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria, however, have said they do not intend to take part in the latest funding round for Ukraine, prompting a warning from the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, that he would block the EU’s seven-year budget unless all countries got onboard.
The four central and eastern countries are net beneficiaries of the EU budget, while Germany is the largest payer and Ukraine’s biggest EU donor.
The EU wants Ukraine’s non-EU allies – such as Norway, the UK and Canada – to find €25bn for Kyiv in 2027.

The EU proposal included provisions “to help other countries to help us”, a senior commission official said. Brussels has proposed that G7 countries that provide new loans get guarantees that the borrowing can be repaid with future profits from Russia’s frozen assets.
The profits from the Russian assets are being used to repay a €45bn loan issued by the G7 to Ukraine in 2024.
after newsletter promotion

Countries with a triple-A credit rating could opt to provide guarantees to the EU budget up to €5bn to expand European borrowing for Ukraine on capital markets. The commission has identified six countries that fall into this category: Australia, Canada, Liechtenstein, Norway, Singapore and Switzerland.

EU officials previously said the UK and other allies needed to do more to support Ukraine in 2027, arguing that the EU was shouldering too much of the burden. The UK subsequently pledged a £10bn economic and military support package for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said: “The UK, Canada, Japan, and Norway have been helping tremendously in our defence of life, and establishing clear rules under which they can provide further aid in conjunction with the EU will help even more.”

Britain said on Wednesday night it would send 1,000 long-range attack drones to Ukraine as part of a further £260m military aid package, a day before prime minister Andy Burnham was due to travel to Berlin to co-chair a meeting of Kyiv’s European allies.

The commitment to support Ukraine’s deep strike campaign into Russia emerged a day after the US argued that Kyiv’s attacks on refineries and warehouses were ineffective and counter-productive, earning criticism from the UK and Germany.
“The UK will do everything we can to ensure Ukraine is able to defend itself,” Burnham said.

articles.title: Catherine visits Mumbai maternity hospital on the last day of royal trip
articles.summary: The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.

blocks.text: The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.
Catherine visited a maternity hospital in Mumbai and was seen comforting a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.
William met actors Kareena Kapoor, Saif Ali Khan and filmmaker Karan Johar during a visit to a film production company.
The couple also met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, with a Kensington Palace spokesperson saying they discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship".

articles.title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
articles.summary:
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on…

blocks.text: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.

Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.

Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

articles.title: She says Russell Brand sexually assaulted her when she was 16. She's waiving her anonymity to speak out
articles.summary: Mia Latter has decided to waive her legal right to anonymity and speak publicly about her teenage relationship with disgraced actor Russell Brand. She's calling for changes to the U.K.'s…

image.caption: Mia Latter says actor Russell Brand sexually assaulted her when she was 16 and he was 30. The pair were in a romantic relationship at the time, and Latter is calling for changes to the U.K.'s age-of-consent laws. (Rob Latour/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

Mia Latter has decided to waive her legal right to anonymity and speak publicly about her teenage relationship with disgraced actor Russell Brand. She's calling for changes to the U.K.'s age-of-consent laws.
Mia Latter is calling for changes to the U.K.'s age-of-consent laws
WARNING: This article contains details of abuse. It may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.
Mia Latter has decided to waive her legal right to anonymity and speak publicly about her teenage relationship with disgraced actor Russell Brand.
The 37-year-old British woman says Brand sexually assaulted her while they were dating when she was 16 and he was 30.

Victims of alleged sexual offences in the U.K. are afforded lifelong anonymity. But in the wake of Brand's high-profile rape trial, Latter says she felt compelled to go on record to advocate for changes to the country's age-of-consent laws.

"That would never have happened if my parents had been able to stop the relationship dead in its tracks to begin with," Latter told As It Happens host Nil Köksal. "They had nowhere to go. The police wouldn't have been able to help them."
In the U.K., people who are 16 and older can consent to sexual activity with an adult of any age who is not in a position of authority over them.

Matter is working with the Close the Consent Gap campaign, which advocates a "staggered" age of consent in which it would be an offence for a person over 20 to engage in sexual activity with a person aged 16–17, unless the age difference is no more than three years.
LISTEN | Interview with Mia Latter:
As It Happens6:44Mia Latter says Russell Brand sexually assaulted her when she was 16. She wants the U.K. to change its age of consent
Brand, 51, was convicted this month on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison. He continues to deny all allegations against him.
Matter's allegations, which were not part of the trial, are under police investigation.
'I told him my age'
Latter, who now lives in California, says she was shopping at Leicester Square in London when she first met Brand. She recognized him from his appearances on MTV.
"I told him my age before we ever went on a date, and he didn't have a problem with it for one moment," she said.

"My mum went to Brand and asked him not to see me. And she wanted to look him in the eye and talk to him about this. And he just was quite defiant and looked at her and just said, 'And what?' Because he knew there was nothing she could do."
Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault. He's maintained his innocence behind bars. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)
The U.K.'s Ministry of Justice says the Law Commission has been tasked with reviewing the country's consent laws.

“Adults abusing imbalances of power, influence or vulnerability to exploit young people is unacceptable and we will always look at what more can be done to protect young people," a ministry spokesperson said.
"Our immediate focus remains on tackling exploitation, supporting victims and ensuring perpetrators are brought to justice."

In Canada, the age of consent is 16, but a 16- or 17-year-old cannot consent to sexual activity if they are dependent on their partner, their partner is in a position of power over them or the relationship is deemed "exploitative."
'Love bombing'
When Latter and Brand first started seeing each other, she says he was very romantic.
"Lots of poetry and, you know, over-the-top declarations of his intentions and how special I was and all of this stuff," she said.

She says she now recognizes this as "love bombing," an abuse tactic that Western University's Learning Network for gender-based violence defines as "a way of exercising control through overwhelming displays of affection, gifts, and praise."
They dated for three months and toward the end of that period, she says he sexually assaulted her. She described the assault as an oral rape.
Russell Brand sentenced: The CBC's Andrew Nichols talks with columnist Katie Glass of The Times

London's Metropolitan Police Service confirmed it launched an investigation into Latter's allegations in January, but says the Crown Prosecution Service advised that "further information was needed before a charging decision could be made."
“We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor," the police said in an email. "However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”
A Crown Prosecution Service spokesperson said it will "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”
CBC reached out to Brand for comment through his lawyers, but did not receive a response.
Why she decided to go on record
Latter previously spoke about her experience under the pseudodyn "Alice" in a 2023 Sunday Times investigation and the subsequent Times/Channel 4 podcast, Dispatches.
During Brand's pre-trial hearing, defence lawyer Ian Winter KC called Dispatches "a work of fiction" and questioned whether the women featured in the documentary actually exist.
That's why Latter decided to go on record.
"It suddenly clicked in my head," Latter said. "I was like, well, I'm a real person and Russell knows who I am.'"
Winter's law firm, Cloth Fair Chambers, did not respond to a request for comment.
The lawyer has since reported himself to his professional regulator after he had a public confrontation with a Sunday Times reporter following Brand's conviction.

items: Between Russell Brand and David Walliams, is this a watershed moment for U.K. comedy?
Russell Brand accused by 6 women of sexual misconduct, assault following rape conviction

blocks.text: Since she first revealed her identity on Saturday in the Times, Latter says she's been on the receiving end of cruel and defamatory comments from Brand's supporters.
But she says she has no regrets.

"I've just been reading the stories that women are sending to me — and that parents are sending to me, and teachers and social workers and foster carers — about the children that are between the ages of 16 and 18 in their lives that they can't protect," she said.
"That's what's really pushing me forward, and it's also reinforcing to me that I did the right thing in going public. Because this is clearly a much bigger issue than even I could have imagined."

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​
Interview with Mia Latter produced by Sarah Melton

articles.title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from freeways across the US after California ban
articles.summary:
The autonomous driving company suspended driverless taxi rides on US highways days after California banned the vehicles on its own freeways

Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides…

blocks.text: Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways across the US indefinitely. The Alphabet subsidiary pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after California banned them from freeways in response to recent traffic incidents.

Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.

blocks.caption: Waymo robotaxi attempts to pass highway patrol cars into controlled traffic zone - loop

blocks.text: A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”. The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn’t say how long it would last.

Waymo’s voluntary suspension came the same day as the California department of motor vehicles banned the company’s robotaxis from the state’s freeways. The ban followed two traffic incidents, including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, a DMV spokesperson, Jonathan Groveman, said in a statement.

The construction zone incident occurred on 5 November, and the second incident, which involved California highway patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.

Video of the 6 November incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.

“The department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on 18 May.
after newsletter promotion
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions”.

California’s restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on the state’s freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions”.

articles.title: Can Anthropic's record breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
articles.summary: Anthropic's hotly anticipated IPO is expected to put it in the top 10 most valuable US companies, but the future is uncertain.

blocks.text: BySimon Jack
Business editor

blocks.caption: Simon Jack

blocks.text: It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
A benchmark valuation
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Daniela Amodei helped set up a rival company to OpenAI

blocks.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images
Daniela Amodei helped set up a rival company to OpenAI
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."
So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.
But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.
It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.

There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.
Public doubts
It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dario Amodei is one of Silicon Valley's big beasts

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Dario Amodei is one of Silicon Valley's big beasts

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.
If Anthropic – and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.
Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.
He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.
Hype and FOMO

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it – the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development – means that buying interest is high.
It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.
With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.
Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.
The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.
Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.
"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

articles.title: Gitxsan hereditary chiefs call for halt to rail cargo as diesel leaks from train derailment along river in B.C.
articles.summary: A second landslide and train derailment into the Skeena River in eight months has reignited calls by the Gitxsan Huwilp Government to immediately stop train hauling in the vicinity of its traditional…

image.caption: CN says initial information suggests the Nov. 17 derailment near Terrace, B.C., was caused by a rockslide. (Carl J. Reibin)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A second landslide and train derailment into the Skeena River in eight months has reignited calls by the Gitxsan Huwilp Government to immediately stop train hauling in the vicinity of its traditional territory.
2nd train derailment in northwest B.C in 8 months threatens food security, says Gitxsan Huwilp Government
Two people were taken to hospital on Tuesday after a Canadian National Railway train carrying forestry products went off the tracks due to a rockslide.
Two locomotives and five railcars carrying multiple containers of forest products derailed approximately 17 kilometres west of Terrace, B.C.
Images from the scene showed several cars off the track, with multiple containers in the water.
2 CN Rail employees injured after train derails near Terrace
CN said diesel has leaked from a locomotive, and crews are working to contain the spill and repair the route. The two employees have since been released from hospital.

It's the second spill recorded in the area this year, after a mudslide derailed grain cars along the Skeena during extreme weather in March, resulting in 7,949 litres of diesel being released, 3,421 of which were "unaccounted for," according to the B.C. government's spill response page.

items: 2 hospitalized after CN Rail train derails into Skeena River near Terrace, B.C.

blocks.text: Prior to that incident, there were no major spill reports along the rail line from Terrace to Prince Rupert over the past decade.

But with two events in such a close timespan, Simogyet Skogam'Lahkx Toby Howard said Tuesday’s incident shows a derailment remains "a clear and present danger" to the food security of the Gitxsan people.
A CN Rail train is seen partially spilled into the Skeena River in northwest B.C. in this photo provided by the Gitxsan Huwilp Government on March 17, 2026. (Gitxsan Huwilp Government)
"The fish in the Skeena feed the eagles, the seals and importantly the Gitxsan people," he said in a release.
"People were transported to hospital, and another train is in the Skeena River — train hauling is dangerous and must stop immediately."
Call for rail moratorium in northwest
Howard added that he feels the Ministry of Transportation downplays the derailments and the possibility of future disasters.
He said hauling needs to stop until the route from Burns Lake to Prince Rupert is inspected and safety can be guaranteed.
"A 103-year-old track has created dangerous conditions for the rail system in our territory," he said.
"Gitxsan Hereditary Chiefs have offered their assistance in identifying the areas of most vulnerability on the line but The Ministry of Transportation has dismissed us."
The B.C. government and related ministries have not commented on the incident prior to the swearing-in of premier designate Lorne Doerkson, instead directing media to its spill response page.
It says "an oil sheen appears to extend approximately 1.3 km downstream," adding that the "quantity of product released remains unconfirmed."

The province considers diesel a "non-persistent oil" as it disperses and evaporates more readily than crude oil. However, it notes diesel can still pose a risk to marine animals and birds if they come into contact with a slick.
In a statement, CN said crews and specialized equipment are on site and recovery operations are underway.
The company is working to contain the spill, remove derailed equipment and prepare for track repairs.
Environmental response measures are in place in the Skeena River to minimize impacts, it added.

items: CN Rail working to clean up cars that toppled into Skeena River amid extreme weather

blocks.text: Other First Nations in the area have also voiced worries about the derailment, including Kitselas and Kitsumkalum.
Kitselas First Nation leadership said it has reached out to CN Rail directly, saying it is "deeply concerned" about the reports that diesel fuel has leaked into the Skeena River.

"The Skeena is a vital lifeline for our community and a major migratory corridor for all wild salmon and other critical aquatic species on the lower river system," said the band council in a statement.
Both Kitsumkalum and Kitselas leadership say they remain in contact with CN and continue to monitor the situation closely.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catherine Garrett is a CBC News reporter based in Terrace, B.C., covering the province's northwest region. Born in Ontario and raised on Haida Gwaii, she has previously worked in Vancouver, Prince George, B.C., and Grande Prairie, Alta. She has received multiple awards for her work, including a Canadian Online Publishing Award. You can contact her at catherine.garrett@cbc.ca.
With files from Andrew Kurjata

articles.title: Cadets being told to stand down as Canada spends billions on defence
articles.summary: The Canadian military has suspended most weekend cadet training and competitions in parts of the country until March, citing budget restraint. Leaked emails reveal mounting financial pressures…

image.caption: Cadets march in a parade following a Remembrance Day ceremony in New Brunswick. Cadets in Ontario and B.C. are facing cutbacks as the Department of National Defence works to hit budget reduction targets. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The Canadian military has suspended most weekend cadet training and competitions in parts of the country until March, citing budget restraint. Leaked emails reveal mounting financial pressures despite billions in new defence spending.
Budget restraint sidelines youth training despite Ottawa's massive investments
The Canadian military has put a halt to most cadet training in various parts of the country because of ongoing budget restraint within the Department of National Defence.
The halt involves weekend training and participation in competitions and will last until the end of the fiscal year in March. Weekly parade nights, however, will continue at least for the time being.

A series of internal emails, obtained by CBC News, outline the decision and paint a picture of an organization struggling to manage the impact of the Defence Department's cuts to operations and support funding.
The Ottawa Citizen was the first to report on the restrictions involving the cadet program. The news was confirmed by a subsequent leak of emails to CBC News.

items: Billions more for defence, but Canada's military still faces an old budget squeeze

blocks.text: "Due to the current fiscal environment, all cadet activities are paused for the remainder of the current fiscal year, ending 31 March 2027, with the exception of weekly parade nights, which may continue at this time," said one leaked email quoting Lt.-Col. Raphael MacKenzie, who commands Ontario's Regional Cadet Support Unit (Central).
No one at the Defence Department was immediately available to comment on the leaked documents.
In mid-October, CBC News was the first to report on the department's internal belt-tightening, which is a knock-on effect from cuts mandated in previous federal budgets.
Department expected to find $459M in savings

The Defence Department has been given tens of billions of new funding by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney. It has been told to focus that extra cash on priority areas, including the purchase of much-needed combat equipment.
At the same time, DND is subject to the demand for operations and maintenance reductions announced by the Trudeau government in 2023 and enacted in the 2024 federal budget.
Those reductions, according to the latest federal budget, are significant.
DND is expected to find $459 million in operational savings this fiscal year, and another $459 million next year.
Last week, CBC News reported on how a reserve unit in southwestern Ontario limited paid participation in Remembrance Day activities because of the budget restraint.
There are also unconfirmed reports of full-time reservists having their three-year contracts cancelled with less than 30 days' notice.
That runs contrary to the latest federal budget's departmental plans report, which downplayed the impact of the internal restraint.
"No job losses are anticipated as a result of these reductions," said the budget report, recently tabled in Parliament.

The department and the Canadian military remain in "a period of growth, supported by significant long-term defence investments that continue to strengthen operational readiness, capabilities and the civilian and military workforce needed to deliver them," the report said.
Defence will enter the 'top rank' of government spending: PBO

Conservative defence critic James Bezan said the reserves and cadets are bearing the brunt of the restraint and the budget chaos makes a mockery of the Liberal government's pledge to invest in defence.
"Mark Carney and the Liberals can't be talking out of both sides of their mouths, saying that they're investing in the armed forces and then cutting operations," Bezan said.
"That reduces our readiness. The Carney cuts are having real impacts on the day-to-day operations of the Canadian Armed Forces."
The restrictions on cadet activities took effect immediately in Ontario, while similar measures will come into force on Nov. 21 in British Columbia.

items: Military budget squeeze limits paid Remembrance Day participation in Ontario

blocks.text: A separate email detailing the restraint in the B.C. region said that cadet leadership is trying to preserve activities that directly support the conduct of weekly training at corps and squadrons and that remains "our priority."
The commanding officer of the Pacific region plans to conduct town halls on Nov. 19 and Nov. 23 to further explain the decision.

"We recognize that this direction will come as a surprise to most and will be disappointing to cadets, families and your teams who have invested considerable time and effort in planning activities for the year ahead," said the second email, dated Nov. 16.
"We share that disappointment. These are not measures that would be taken if the resources were available to sustain the program as planned."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
