articles.title: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.summary: Ukraine's latest strike on the Kerch Bridge has disrupted a key transport link between Russia and Crimea. Beyond the damage, the attack could have serious consequences for Russian military logistics…

image.caption: Debris from the destroyed bridge arch is obstructing the main shipping route linking the Black Sea and the Sea of AzovImage: Ukrainian Security Service/AFP

blocks.text: It had been a year and a half since Ukraine last attacked the 19-kilometer-long Kerch Bridge connecting Russian-annexed Crimea with Russia's Krasnodar region.

Now, Ukraine has struck again. The attack during the night of November 17 caused the highway section of the bridge to collapse into the sea. As a result, shipping traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov has also been disrupted.

Russia's ministry of transport announced a "temporary suspension" of road and rail traffic on the bridge, though later, rail services were resumed. Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." It was only after this announcement that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed the attack.

The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula, an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.

It has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. The most well-known strike occurred in October 2022, when an explosives-laden truck detonated on the bridge, causing extensive damage and several months of traffic restrictions. The most recent attack took place in June 2025, when the SBU reported that an underwater support structure was blown up.
A long time in the making

The latest Ukrainian operation lasted about a month, and consisted of seven distinct phases. "First, the SBU and armed forces systematically neutralized the enemy's air defense system. After that, the direct attack on the bridge began," says the SBU Telegram channel.
Some Russian military bloggers claim that the attack was carried out with the support of Ukraine's Western allies, or at least using their equipment and weapons.

blocks.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin (center) personally oversaw the bridge's constructionImage: YURI KOCHETKOV/AFP

blocks.text: Ukraine has not confirmed this. It has instead pointed out that various Ukrainian-made weapons were used in the attack, ranging from a variety of drones, to FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptun missiles. British daily The Times has cited Ukrainian military sources, saying that Ukraine attacked the bridge without the support of SpaceX's satellite network system Starlink. There has been no confirmation of this so far.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, described the strike as a response to Russian attacks: "Russia is attacking our infrastructure every day, particularly bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region." He said "we are rebuilding our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that the war always returns to where it began."
Ukraine hits strategic Russian bridge to Crimea
The impact on shipping

After the attack, pictures and videos of the bridge were shared on social media. The Krimskij Veter Telegram channel has highlighted damage to the railroad link and questioned why Russian authorities have opted to resume train services.
The Kerch Strait shipping channel is also completely blocked by debris. "This brings road traffic to a standstill, but also shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the channel writes.

Indeed, the Kerch Strait navigational channel is merely 120 meters wide, writes Mychajlo Hontschar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" on Facebook. "The strait is shallow, only three to five meters deep."

As early as the 19th century, the seabed was dredged to allow heavier ships to pass from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and vice versa. "Now, Vladimir Putin's bridge-building efforts have brought shipping to an indefinite standstill," Hontschar said.

Not only will river-sea vessels no longer be able to leave the waters of the Sea of Azov, the Don, and the Volga, but boats and small ships from the Black Sea fleet and the Caspian flotilla based in Novorossiysk will also be unable to do so.
The military consequences
Many pro-Kremlin Telegram channels have been quick to claim that the bridge does not play an important role in the Russian army's logistics or in supplying Crimea.
The Dva Mayora (Two Majors) channel quotes the "Deputy President of the Republic of Crimea," Olga Kurlayeva, who described the bridge as a "purely civilian structure."

Ukrainian military experts interviewed by DW, on the other hand, point to the systematic disruption of Russian logistics. These efforts also included regular attacks on the R-80 highway leading through Russian-occupied territories of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.

Russia cannot replace the Kerch Bridge with any other land connection, says Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military expert with the Information Resistance Group that seeks to counter disinformation. He expects the damaged bridge will cause supply problems for the Russian armed forces: "If there is a resource shortage during attacks or in defense, then either the attacks or the defense will fail."

blocks.caption: The bridge's road-traffic arch has collapsed into the seaImage: Ukrainian Security Service/AFP

blocks.text: That is why he does not rule out a decline in attacks from occupied Crimea on the rest of Ukraine. "There are many launch pads for kamikaze drones in Crimea — in the Hvardijsk area, at Cape Chauda and in Balaklava," Kovalenko told DW. "From there, many drones are launched toward Odesa, Mykolaiv, and the right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. They also fly over Crimea en route toward Ukraine. Then there are attacks using Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as Zircon and Oniks missiles, guided missiles, and glide bombs. And while they don't originate in Crimea, they are brought over via the Kerch Bridge."
A bad look for Putin

Kovalenko says the bridge strike has dealt a serious blow to Vladimir Putin's standing. It comes at a sensitive time as Putin is about to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China.

Memes and witty comments about the bridge abound on X. Meanwhile, the Russian president's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has promised to rebuild the bridge and assured that it will be "even better than before."

Andrii Korezkyj of the Kyiv University of Transportation, however, says this is not likely to happen anytime soon. "All in all, I would estimate that it would take between one and a half and three years [to rebuild]," Korezkyj told DW, adding, "I don't think they'll let the Russians build another [bridge] arch like that near the Ukrainian border without interference."
Pro-Russian commentators, known as Z-bloggers, agree with this view. "Unlike in 2022 and 2023, the Ukrainian armed forces are now able to launch strikes against floating cranes and repair teams."
"Even installing a pre-assembled arch under these conditions would constitute a challenging task," writes the pro-Kremlin Rybar Telegram channel.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Hegseth boasts about Maduro’s capture while vowing to deepen US military cooperation with Venezuela
articles.summary:
The US defense secretary called the former president’s capture the ‘most sophisticated military operation’ in Latin American history

Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since…

blocks.text: Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela.​ Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.

“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.

In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.

“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.

Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.

“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.

During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.

But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”

Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.

Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.

“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.

Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”

Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.

But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

articles.title: US Pentagon chief Hegseth signs military deal in Venezuela
articles.summary: On a visit to Caracas, Pete Hegseth signed a deal that signifies the "reestablishment of our defense partnership." US-Venezuela ties were strained for years until US troops ousted ex-President…

image.caption: Hegseth spoke with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez during the visit Image: Miraflores Palace/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Venezuela on Wednesday, met with the country's interim authorities and also signed a military cooperation deal with the Latin American country.
What do we know so far about Hegseth's trip?
The Pentagon did not release any information on Hegseth's trip or confirm the visit, although it was broadcast on Venezuelan state media.

The visit comes after US forces in January ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and took him along with his wife to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Since then, US President Donald Trump has backed acting President Delcy Rodriguez to lead the country.

blocks.caption: Hegseth also met with new Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, who had belonged to a party opposing Maduro  Image: Miraflores Palace/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Both Rodriguez and Hegseth touted the new military agreement between the two countries at the presidential palace in Caracas.
Rodriguez said the deal would strengthen training for the Venezuelan military while facilitating access to new technologies. She said this would allow the two nations to "face common threats."
Hegseth said the US sees the deal "as a reestablishment of our defense partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries."
The agreement includes intelligence sharing between the two nations in addition to joint training.

The Pentagon chief said the US seeks "to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders."
Hegseth said Wednesday that since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner."
How have US-Venezuela relations changed?

US-Venezuela relations were strained under Maduro, who had taken office in 2013. In 2019, Maduro cut off Venezuela's formal diplomatic relations with the US after Trump's first administration recognized Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaido as the country's interim president.
Is the US looting Venezuela?

After the ouster of Maduro, the Trump administration urged Venezuela to comply with demands such as US access to the Venezuelan oil market. Trump had threatened Rodriguez, who was Venezuela's vice president, with a "fate worse than Maduro" if she didn't cooperate with Washington.
Trump has later praised Rodriguez as a "terrific person" who is doing a "great job."

Under Rodriguez, Venezuela has released political prisoners and facilitated the shipments of oil to the US, with the US then controlling the proceeds and returning the money under an energy deal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been overseeing Venezuela's transition and is in close contact with Rodriguez.

Elections after Maduro's ouster are expected at some point in Venezuela, but with Rodriguez's government acting favorably towards the US, it's unclear whether they would happen anytime soon. Nobel Prize winner and opposition leader Maria Corina Machado recently urged elections after arriving in Venezuela.

articles.title: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.summary: Hamas condemns the incursion, which the Israeli military says is dismantling a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.

blocks.text: Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.
Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.
It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.
Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.

At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Nearly 300,000 people sign petition demanding U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's removal
articles.summary: More than 285,000 people have signed a petition asking the federal government to remove U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra from Canada.

image.caption: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has made several comments supporting U.S. President Donald Trump's position that Canada should become the 51st state. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
More than 285,000 people have signed a petition asking the federal government to remove U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra from Canada.
Government will have 45 days to respond after petition is tabled
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 18, 2026 2:45 PM EST | Last Updated: November 18
The petition accuses Hoekstra of making public statements that have undermined Canadian and U.S. relations and says he described the 2025 Canadian federal election campaign as "anti-American."
The petition says Hoekstra accused Canada of interfering in U.S. domestic politics while making repeated statements on Canadian politics "inconsistent with diplomatic protocol."
The petition closes to new signatures on Wednesday and most of those who signed live in Ontario or British Columbia.

items: Tens of thousands of Canadians call for U.S. Ambassador Hoekstra to be expelled

blocks.text: Now that the petition has received more than the mandatory 500 signatures it needed to proceed, former Green Party leader Elizabeth May can present it to the House of Commons.
Once it's presented to the House, the government has 45 calendar days to respond.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alyssa Wheeler is a reporter with The Canadian Press.

articles.title: EU to reject UK talks on longer-term ties pending clarity from Burnham on next steps
articles.summary:
Diplomats says piecemeal approach of resets coming to an end and they want government decision on whether it will seek to reverse Brexit

The EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy…
articles.byline: Pippa Crerar, Lisa O’Carroll and Jessica Elgot

blocks.text: The EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy Burnham about the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc until the government has decided whether it wants to proceed with reversing Brexit, diplomats have said.

European capitals are also warning they have reached the end of the line for piecemeal “reset” summits with the UK and want the prime minister to focus on his next steps domestically before they proceed.

But they suggested a joint statement after a summit this Friday would signal that further discussions would follow on the UK’s entry to the EU’s energy single markets, irregular migration and a closer defence and security relationship.
“Clarity is what we need more than anything from the UK. Don’t come back until you know what you want. Work out what your options really are and then come to negotiate,” one EU diplomat said.

“The prime minister needs to bring the public with him. We can’t have another negotiation based on just half the country. We’ll only put the effort in if we know it’s not going to change down the line.”
Burnham is expected to set out his own next steps after the summit on Monday, including his hopes for a “national conversation” on what a closer relationship might look like.

With less than 48 hours before the Brussels summit, negotiators were still racing to finalise Friday’s agreement. A leaked draft seen by the Guardian shows continued disagreement over demands by the EU that the UK commit to aligning with the bloc’s trade defence measures, such as tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, in exchange for inclusion in Made in Europe legislation.
The text shows the UK is pushing for a weaker commitment, only promising an “aim to protect supply chains consistently across our markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention”.

A Cabinet Office source said Made in Europe language was “the highest jeopardy” in the negotiations, while an EU official suggested it was the part of the discussions most likely to go “down to the wire” on Friday.

Though there is a formal commitment to annual reset summits, senior EU diplomats say the current approach, designed by Keir Starmer, will quickly “reach its limits” and more “mini deals” do not make sense.
One said the “piecemeal approach is coming to an end” and that Burnham’s intentions for the UK’s long-term relationship created a natural juncture for the EU too.
Another said: “It is like a buffet: you can choose to nibble on one or two dishes to start, but at a certain point you have to go for the whole of the buffet.”
One EU diplomat said there would be a “pause for reflection” after the Friday summit.
Burnham has said there is no rush to decide on the longer-term relationship, as he comes under pressure from within his own party to slow the pace of pursuing of closer ties.

He is now not expected to set out the full range of options for the future relationship – the status quo, customs union, single market or full rejoin – until he announces his 10-year plan in December.

Sources said the government was considering holding a year-long “national conversation” in 2027, including town halls and citizens assemblies, ahead of deciding which route to pursue before the next election.

However, the potential length of that debate has alarmed Brussels officials, who were caught off-guard by the launch of the new pro-Brexit campaign group Stay Out, set up by architects of the Vote Leave campaign.

One EU diplomat said: “The government would spend the year making evidence-based arguments about each of the four options, while Boris Johnson and Michael Gove and Nigel Farage will spend it shouting about traitors.”

After the reset deal is agreed on Friday, it will be enacted by the European partnership bill, covering the deals on food and agriculture, emissions trading and youth mobility. It is expected to be introduced before Christmas, with legislation laid possibly as soon as next week.

EU diplomats said the two sides were expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 people a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each other’s territories. Originally, the UK had pitched for 50,000 and then 80,000, while Brussels has consistently sought a higher number.

Both sides have agreed that tuition fees for European students coming to the UK should be discussed at a later date, although there have been attempts by some member states to link the debate to the ratification of the whole reset deal.

Senior Labour figures are already beginning their push to have a full rejoin on the table. The former business secretary Peter Kyle said Burnham should fight the next election on a promise to rejoin the EU, with voters given a referendum on the outcome of any deal.

Kyle, who was a key member of Keir Starmer’s cabinet, said the “only way through” the challenges of the domestic political debate was for the government to offer voters the choice to accept or reject any agreement.

He is the latest senior Labour MP to publicly wade into the Brexit debate, after the former foreign secretary David Lammy said the party should go into the next election clear that its intention was to rejoin.
Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, has also said Britain’s future should be back in the bloc, arguing that leaving had made the UK “poorer, weaker and less secure”.

articles.title: Would Ukraine trade land for NATO membership or protection?
articles.summary: The US is exploring whether Ukraine would cede parts of Donetsk province still under its control in return for NATO membership or protection. Experts warn the idea is risky.

image.caption: Trading Donbass for NATO protection — a dangerous move for Kyiv?Image: Ralf Hirschberger/dpa/picture-alliance

blocks.text: The US has asked Ukraine whether it would be willing to cede Donetsk province to Russia in return for NATO membership. Together, Donetsk and Luhansk constitute the so-called Donbas region. Russia currently controls most of Luhansk province, and large swathes of Donetsk, though Ukraine continues holding a number of major cities there, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.

So far, no concrete proposal had been put forward, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said he would publicly discuss the matter once the US and NATO member states had agreed on the plan, stressing that he could not make any such decision "on his own." Zelenskyy also said any potential agreement would go ahead "without recognizing Russia's occupation of these territories."

The Ukrainian leader said the US was talking about guarantees similar to those enshrined in Articles 4 and 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, though did not envision US troops on Ukrainian soil. Article 4 provides for consultations among member states in the event of imminent threats, while Article 5 stipulates that an attack on one state is considered an attack on all. The US, however, has said it pictures bilateral guarantees for Ukraine similar to those established with Israel and certain Middle Eastern countries.

Russia has yet to comment on these proposals, with President Putin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stating that "we maintain our position that, in the interest of the peace process, it is not appropriate to disclose details of the talks between us and the Americans."

blocks.caption: US special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner recently met Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (right) in DublinImage: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: Budapest Memorandum 2.0?
Experts interviewed by DW are skeptical of the land-for-security-guarantees idea, objecting that the US cannot uphold such an arrangement on its own.

"It seems to me that this is what happens to normal diplomacy when it's been run by real estate agents who are used to selling people something that doesn't really exist," Oleksandr Kraiev of the North America-Israel Research Program at Ukraine's Ukrainian Prism think tank tells DW. He says that at least half of NATO's member states have reservations about Ukraine's accession.

"We'll just end up with a second Budapest Memorandum, it'll just carry a different name," Kraiev told DW. The original 1994 Budapest Memorandum stipulated that Russia, the US and UK respect Ukraine's independence and sovereignty in its existing borders and refrain from the threat or use of force to change its territorial integrity. Ukraine in return committed to giving up all nuclear weapons.
The Budapest Memorandum, however, did not contain any commitment by the UK or US to defend Ukraine in the event of an attack.
A dangerous precedent

Most experts interviewed by DW are critical of the idea of holding a referendum to let ordinary Ukrainians decide whether their country should hand over full control of Donetsk province in exchange for NATO membership.

This is because ceding territory would not only violate Ukraine's constitution and harm its national interests, but would also undermine a world order "in which borders cannot be redrawn by force," Oleksandr Khara of Ukraine's Centre for Defence Strategies told DW. "It doesn't matter whether the citizens of Ukraine vote for or against such a proposal," Khara said, adding that any such referendum would set "a very dangerous precedent."

A survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KISS) conducted between October 8 and 16 found that 61% of respondents categorically reject withdrawing troops from Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donbas, such as cities like Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, even in exchange for US and European security guarantees. 35% of respondents said they would begrudgingly accept a land-for-security deal.
Donbas dilemma: Why Russia and Ukraine won't let go
What are the alternatives?
Defense analyst Khara doubts a bilateral agreement between Ukraine and the US, akin to those established between the US and Israel, would guarantee Kyiv any more support than it presently receives.

"This concerns financial support, joint weapons production and development, and the training of Ukrainian troops — everything that falls below the threshold of collective security," Khara told DW. "It is good that these commitments — security agreements, political declarations, and the allocation of funds in the budgets of the countries supporting us — are set out in writing, at least for the next five years." Yet to prevent another war, Khara believes that ideally, Ukraine needs "a nuclear shield," specifically, a "strategic one from the US" and a "tactical one from Europe."

Ukrainian experts already floated to the idea of an alternative security arrangement to NATO members in December 2023, says Sergiy Solodkyy of Ukraine's New Europe research center. The arrangement would see Ukraine join the alliance within its internationally recognized borders, though specific protocols would stipulate that only territories under Kyiv's control would be defended.
This arrangement could be modeled on the German case, where West Germany became a member of NATO first, while East Germany joined the alliance only after German reunification.

West Germany never gave up on reunification, Solodkyy told DW. "That means we, too, should not give up on our territory or recognize the border." That is why he says the land-for-security deal proposed to Ukraine is unacceptable.
"This is a trap that Russia and the US negotiators are trying to lure the Ukrainian side into," Solodkyy told DW.
This article was translated from German

articles.title: Israel launches new ground operation in Gaza
articles.summary: Israel has said its military is targeting Hamas infrastructure in central Gaza and urged civilians to avoid the area. The fight is unfolding against the backdrop of a dire food and shelter situation…

image.caption: Israel and Hamas have carried out limited attacks since an October 2025 ceasefire ended large-scale operations [File photo: November 2025]Image: IDF/GPO/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israel says its military is involved in operations on Wednesday in central Gaza in an effort to dislodge Hamas militants.
France's AFP news agency reported "intense Israeli artillery shelling amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes."

A statement from the Israeli military (IDF) said, "The IDF launched a precise operation within Gaza earlier today west of the Yellow Line to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip."
The Yellow Line in Gaza was established in an October 2025 ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, and separates Israeli and Hamas-controlled territory.

On Wednesday, COGAT, an Israeli military body responsible for civilian matters in the Palestinian territories warned international aid agencies and Palestinian civilians to avoid areas near the Al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps and Gaza's main thoroughfare, the Salah al-Din road.
Has the war in Gaza weakened Israel?
Why are the IDF and Hamas still fighting?

Palestinian medics told Reuters news agency that one person had been killed in an Israeli airstrike in central Gaza and that two more had been killed in separate incidents unfolding in Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.

Hamas — which is listed as a terrorist organization by Israel, the US, Germany, the EU and others — blasted the Israeli operation, calling it "a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement and confirmation that the occupation has reneged on its obligations."
Israel's military countered that it was reacting to Hamas ceasefire violations and the group's attempts to rearm.

The October 2025 ceasefire halted major operations, but both sides have continued to carry out limited attacks. Gaza health authorities report at least 1,600 Palestinian deaths and Israel reports the loss of fewer than 10 soldiers since the ceasefire went into effect.

In all, Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed inside Gaza during Israel's retaliation for Hamas' October 7, 2023, assault — which killed roughly 1,200 Israelis, most of whom were civilians.
Israelis demand accountability for October 7
How dire is the situation for Palestinian civilians in Gaza?
Beyond the threat of violent gunfire and airstrikes, civilians in Gaza continue to face ongoing food insecurity and lack of adequate shelter as winter approaches.

On Tuesday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the UN's World Food Programme (WFP) warned that funding shortfalls and access restrictions put untold numbers of Palestinian lives at risk.
Currently, more than 1.7 million Gazans are displaced, with IOM and WFP saying 1.4 million face acute hunger and 1.98 million require shelter assistance.

With Gaza's infrastructure decimated by years of Hamas mismanagement and pounding Israeli attacks, more than 80% of Palestinians are unemployed, meaning they cannot afford food and have been forced to burn garbage to try to keep warm.

"Families in Gaza are facing their first sleepless nights of a very long winter ahead," said WFP Palestine Country Director Shaun Hughes. "Unless we get immediate support to scale up the humanitarian response, we risk this becoming not only a shelter crisis but also a deeper food security crisis."
Gaza's children bear lasting scars three years into war

articles.title: Muslims to outnumber Christians by 2035, research shows
articles.summary: Pew Research Center projections show that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. Researchers say differences in fertility rates account for the change.

image.caption: Both Islam and Christianity are growing in size, but the number of Muslims is growing faster, according to new researchImage: Ismael Adnan Yaqoob/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Muslims are going to outnumber Christians by 2035, according to projections from the Washington-based Pew Research Center.
Pew said that while both religions are growing, Islam is growing faster than Christianity.
The main reason is Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups, according to the study.
"It's the babies,” Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett told the AP news agency.

Pew data shows that Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children between 2020 and 2025, compared with 2.5 for Christian women. For all other women, the average was 1.6, lower than the 2.1 needed to replace each generation.
Why Gen Z men are embracing Catholicism in the US
According to the center's estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020.

New projections show that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. If current trend persists, the global Muslim population is projected to exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the number of Christians is expected to fall just short of 3 billion.
The US will no longer be Christian majority in 2070, Pew estimates
According to the report, if recent trends continue, by 2070:

items: More than half of the world's Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa. This was, again, attributed to the region's high fertility and rising life expectancy.
An African country, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, will surpass the United States as the country with the greatest number of Christians.
The United States will no longer have a Christian majority, though Christians will remain the biggest religious group in the country.
Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia, which currently has the most Muslims.
Hindus will increase most in absolute numbers in India, but they will grow faster in countries outside India, including the US
The overall populations of China, Japan and South Korea will shrink, and their Buddhist populations will drop by more than half.
Most countries will have more religiously unaffiliated people than they do now. But the increase will be entirely offset by population decline in China, where most religious "nones" currently live.
62% of all Jews will live in Israel, up from 46% in 2020.
Although the number of Hindus and Jews will grow in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population.
Europe's population will shrink by 17%. The number of Christians will drop by 35.8%, from 505 million to 324 million, while the continent's Muslim population will increase from 6% to 13%.

blocks.text: Growth is not at the expense of Christians, says Pew researcher

Alan Cooperman, Pew's director of religion research, told AP news agency that most of the projected growth of Muslims and Christians was occurring in countries where they already are the majority. He says conversion plays only a minor role.

"I don't think this is a situation in which the growth of Muslims is coming at the expense of Christians. I do worry about mischief being made with headlines or narratives that take this finding and portray it as sort of a clash where Christians are losing to Muslims,” he said.
Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specializing in religious demographics, said inter-religious relations are "extremely important" in light of the trends.

"I hope people seek opportunities for greater inter-religious education. Personal contact is important — when people have personal relationships across religious differences, it ‘humanizes' the ‘other' in fruitful ways," she said.

articles.title: Markwayne Mullin defends move to take government plane to football game amid flight stoppage – US politics live
articles.summary: The secretary of homeland security flew to attend a college game Saturday, after thousands of flights were cancelled
articles.byline: Lucy Campbell (now); Shrai Popat and Tom Ambrose (earlier)

blocks.text: Mullin defends move to take government plane to college football game amid nationwide grounding in House hearing

During today’s hearing Markwayne Mullin defended his decision to take a government plane to attend a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas on Saturday, while thousands of flights had been cancelled and the airspace closed during the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) nationwide grounding over the weekend.

“You want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior because I wanted to be a good uncle,” Mullin said, following questions from Congressman Bennie Thompson, the committee’s top Democrat.
Mullin went further, and said that had he not traveled to the game it could have created “confusion” because he was due to meet Louisiana governor Jeff Landry.
Mullin added that his absence might have shown “distrust that we’re not even willing to fly” after the FAA reopened the airspace.

“We had discussions at 10 o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it,” the homeland security secretary said. “We were saying our skies were completely open. On Saturday alone, 36,000 planes flew and flew safely. Before I took off, the airspace had been open for almost 24 hours.”

Mullin noted that he paid for the trip himself because it was for non-official business, even though he is required to use the government aircraft for security reasons, and scolded Democrats for their line of questioning.
“The hypocrisy from you and from the members that want to make a big deal out of it … you guys would have done the same thing, but you would have called it a campaign event,” he said.

blocks.text: And responding to the nomination of Hakeem Jeffries to be the next – and first Black – House speaker, Chuck Schumer told reporters:

double quotation markI’m so glad he was elected by such an overwhelming margin. He’s going to be a great speaker. It’s historic. I’ve known him from the very early days when he was even running for Congress, and I look forward to working with him together.
'I will be elected majority leader': Schumer expresses confidence he has the votes to beat Van Hollen
Chuck Schumer, the current Senate minority leader facing a challenge for majority leader from Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, also expressed confidence he would get the position.
Asked by a reporter if he was concerned about his election, Schumer replied: “No. I will be elected majority leader. I’m confident we have the votes.”

In that case, he was asked, should Van Hollen give up his bid? “That’s going to be up to him,” Schumer said. “I think what we all want to do is roll up our sleeves together, everybody, and deliver for the American people. That’s what we’re focused on. That’s what we’re focused on.”
Schumer calls Peltola's historic win in Alaska 'an exclamation point on a great election year'
Celebrating Mary Peltola’s historic win in Alaska, Chuck Schumer described her victory “an exclamation point on what has been a great election year”.

Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.
“We now have a margin of nine Democratic senators,” Schumer told reporters. “This is the greatest landslide in midterms in over 70 years.”
He said the Democrats had won due to “great candidates like Peltola” but also “because we focused on what the American people cared about: lowering their costs, ending corruption, ending the chaos.”
He went on: “The real work starts today. We’ve won the election. We’ve won the American people’s votes, but now we have to earn their trust.”

blocks.caption: Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer speaks to reporters outside the US Capitol. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In July, an ICE agent shot and killed the 25-year-old father during a traffic stop in Biddeford, 15 minutes from Scarborough, just days after an agent killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas.

The shooting renewed calls for accountability in the agency. In particular, it renewed scrutiny over ICE’s hiring practices after it came to light that the officer that killed Guerrero, David Brouillette, had a troubling history of violent behavior, including past complaints of domestic violence and abuse, as well as mental health issues. Brouillette, who was hired during a federal recruitment surge, also has a record of deep-seated anti-immigrant hostility.

Magaziner asked Mullin how many ICE agents were currently on the streets who had not completed full background checks. Mullin said they had all completed training, to which Magaziner reminded him was not his question. Mullin course-corrected: “Every ICE agent we have in service right now have full background checks.” The ones that don’t are on administrative leave until they do, he added.

Magaziner, of Rhode Island, pointed out to Mullin that Brouillette’s background check had not been completed when he fatally shot Guerrero, nor had he completed standardized training when he was “put on the street with a mask and a gun” by the Trump administration. “He was put on the street after completing just an online course, he didn’t even do any of the in-person training in Georgia,” Magaziner said. “Has everyone who is out there on the street today completed the full 13-week in-person training?”
Mullin said they had, and those who haven’t had been put on administrative leave. He said there had also been additional training introduced.
He couldn’t answer how many people had been put on the street who hadn’t had the full training, and then appeared to defer responsibility to his predecessor.
double quotation markUnfortunately, congressman, there were some decisions that were made before I was secretary that we were having to undo.
You can watch a clip of the exchange here.

blocks.caption: DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin testifies before the House homeland security committee. Photograph: Nathan Howard/Reuters

blocks.text: Cris Seda Chabrier
Canadian prime minister Mark Carney emphasized Canada’s efforts to strengthen their own sovereignty by moving away from dependence on the US economy, infrastructure and defense.

He spoke to DealBook, a New York Times summit with global leaders, from China, where he has struck a deal with Xi Jinping to reduce tariffs between the two countries – a sign that Carney is breaking with US policy towards China. The two countries have been at odds since Donald Trump returned to the White House two years ago, and has continually threatened to annex Canada and has placed tariffs on Canadian goods.

Canada is also seeking closer ties to Europe by increasing trade, collaborating on defense, research and intelligence. For example, Europe and Canada are trying to launch their own satellite system to reduce dependency on Elon Musk’s Starshield.
More trade deals are being struck with other countries, including the Philippines and India.
Carney emphasized that the US remains a key ally, but said Canada’s diversification could give them the upper hand in talks to better their relationship with the US.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” Carney said.

The Canadian prime minister did add, however, that Trump is “very different” behind closed doors. “He’s very personable,” Carney said, despite his fraught relationship with the US president. “He listens a lot more in private.”

blocks.caption: Ariana Baio

blocks.text: Ariana Baio

All three national security officials testifying to the House homeland security committee unequivocally said the recent cyber outages were not related, nor were they the result of malicious cyber activity.

Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said: “Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”
Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland Security secretary, noted that his team has seen, “nothing that would indicate they are related”.

“Our cyber experts have been engaged in day one in all of these incidents, and I want to be very clear on this on this point: there is no indication whatsoever that there is any malicious cyber activity related to any of those incidents,” Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, told lawmakers.
'While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done': incoming progressives vote against Hakeem Jeffries bid for House speaker
Of those who voted against Jeffries’ nomination, seven incoming members of the left-flank explained their decision to not support the current minority leader in his nomination for speaker.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” Democratic members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez said in a joint statement.
House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be first Black speaker
House Democrats have nominated current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries as their candidate for speaker in the next Congress.
My colleague Chris Stein reports that, according to a person familiar, Jeffries received 251 yes votes of 262 cast, and 11 members voted no on his nomination.
Jeffries faced no opposition in his candidacy to lead the House, and will face a full chamber vote in the new year, when Republicans will be in the minority.
Rebecca Bailey
The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a separate meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official.
The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
If confirmed, it would be their first bilateral since they met in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to reach a deal on the war in Ukraine.
Trump had already suggested he might meet with Putin, as well as with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, but neither option had been added to his official schedule.
FBI director Kash Patel was called out by Republican Andrew Garbarino, the chair of the House homeland security committee, within minutes of the hearing beginning on Wednesday.
Garbarino began the hearing saying it was “disappointing” that Patel refused to testify to the committee.

“Despite repeated attempts over the span of several months, between then and now, to find any date when he could testify, director made clear that he had no intention of appearing. Director Patel’s refusal to testify marks a significant departure from well-established committee precedent,” Garbarino said.
Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the committee, echoed Garbarino’s concerns.
Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, is testifying to the committee instead.

As we noted earlier, a House homeland security hearing is under way with the department secretary, Markwayne Mullin, deputy FBI director Christopher Raia and director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, all testifying before lawmakers.

articles.title: Fiona, the hippo famous for surviving, is on 24-hour medical watch after eating a hat
articles.summary: A beloved hippopotamus named Fiona is on 24-hour medical watch after eating a hat that was tossed into her enclosure.

image.caption: Fiona, a baby Nile hippopotamus, swims in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden on June 26, 2018. Fiona ate a hat that was tossed into her enclosure about 10 days ago and is receiving medical care, the zoo posted online. (John Minchillo/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
A beloved hippopotamus named Fiona is on 24-hour medical watch after eating a hat that was tossed into her enclosure.
Hippo at Cincinnati Zoo is being treated for dehydration, nausea and pain
A beloved hippopotamus named Fiona is on 24-hour medical watch after eating a knit hat that was tossed into her enclosure.

Now the nine-year-old hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, who became a social media darling after she was born prematurely and survived against all odds, is being treated for dehydration, nausea and pain, a staff member said in a social media update posted Tuesday.
The incident happened about 10 days ago. At first, Fiona was asymptomatic, the staff member said, adding that "she's large enough that a small hat should be passing through."
But after a few days her appetite decreased.
Staff sedated her, ran an ultrasound and gave her rectal fluids but she still hasn't passed the hat. Now, they've giving her anti-nauseants, painkillers and medications to encourage her to eat.
"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos," the staff member said.
"The best bet for Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own."
A social media update on Fiona the hippo posted by the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden on Nov. 17, 2026. (@CincinnatiZoo/Instagram)

Staff sedated her for more diagnostics this week, gave her more fluids and enemas and used a 2.7-metre scope to give Fiona a colonoscopy — but couldn't reach the hat. An ultrasound showed some bunching in her intestines, the zoo added.
"At this point, what we can do is supportive care," the staff member said.
"We're trying to give her all her favourite foods in hope she'll keep passing things through."

blocks.text: The cap got into Fiona's habitat after it was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught by a ceiling fan that catapulted it through a small opening above the area's viewing windows, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told The Canadian Press.
In another social media post about the incident, zoo staff asked visitors to help keep animals safe by securing their belongings and taking extra care near habitats.
"Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a zoo staff member immediately," the zoo wrote.
CBC News has reached out to the zoo for more information.
Fiona eats her specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning three years old in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden on Jan. 23, 2020. (John Minchillo/The Associated Press)
Famous for surviving
Fiona weighed just 13 kilograms when she was born six weeks prematurely in 2017, the zoo previously posted. Most hippos are born weighing between 23 and 50 kilograms.
"She is the smallest hippo to ever survive," the zoo said.

Her fight to survive grabbed international attention. Fans followed her progress online and she became so popular that books were written about her. She also inspired a line of beer, all sorts of clothing and an ice cream flavor.
Fiona sleeps in her enclosure on June 26, 2018. (John Minchillo/The Associated Press)

Now, her fans around the world are following her care, many using the hashtag #teamfiona. Several other zoos and aquariums from Kansas to Honolulu commented on the Cincinnati Zoo's health update, urging Fiona to keep fighting and to pass the hat.
"We are rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life," the zoo wrote online.
"You got this Fiona!! Get that hat out girl!" a fan commented.
"Please poop, Fiona," commented another person.

articles.title: What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
articles.summary: When "GTA VI" is released on November 19, millions of people worldwide will rush to their consoles to play it. How has this video game created such a cross-generational buzz?

image.caption: Lucia and Jason are the protagonists of 'Grand Theft Auto VI': For the first time in the franchise's main titles, gamers can play as a womanImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: "Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.

"GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records. The hype around it is unparalleled. No game in history has clocked so many pre-orders. It's thought that around 10 million people have already purchased it. There's no denying it: "GTA VI" is a global cultural phenomenon.

A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game. The file is so large that downloading it can take several days, depending on the internet connection. Providers have already registered a significant spike in data traffic.
As soon as the game is unlocked, players can start speeding through the fictional US metropolis of Vice City in a stylish sports car with criminal couple Jason and Lucia.
Miami gets cast as Vice City

To mark the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," its real-life inspiration — Miami — is getting a full-scale "Vice City" makeover. This promotional push includes the Miami Heat basketball team stepping onto the hardwood in custom "Vice City" jerseys for a home game, a local festival featuring artists from the game's official soundtrack, and roadside "Vice City" signage installed across the area.

blocks.caption: Vice City is a fictionalized representation of the US metropolis of MiamiImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Expectations for "GTA VI" are sky-high. Nearly 5,000 people have been working on the game for more than 10 years. Development costs are estimated at around $1 billion (€900 million).

"Based on those figures alone — as well as the series' extremely successful and popular track record — this can certainly be described as a truly exceptional release," says Rudolf Thomas Inderst, cultural studies scholar and professor of Game Design and Game Studies at Germany's Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences.

When such an effort is put into a product, it's only natural for people to expect great things, he adds. Inderst is expecting "GTA VI" to showcase the absolute best of what modern gaming can do across gameplay, storytelling, visuals and tech.
Social satire and gameplay freedom

This video game series has been around for almost three decades, setting new standards through its different versions. A biting satire on US society and the American dream, "GTA" parodies politics, culture and the media.

The game is also renowned for its gameplay freedom and spectacularly staged chaos in a crazy world where players can do whatever they please. Shoot down helicopters with a bazooka, go to the hairdresser's, take a stroll on the beach, go to a nightclub, take part in car races and much more.

blocks.caption: Pure escapism: In Vice City, there's shooting and dancingImage: Rockstar Games/dpa Picture Alliance

blocks.text: What makes it a standout among video games is how its NPCs — non-player characters, those not being controlled by a human player — are brought to life. They respond based on a player's interactions with them, displaying individualized behaviors and traits ranging from fear to hostility. "GTA VI" has an estimated 600,000 animations for the civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.
'Grand Theft Auto,' a long-running hit

"GTA VI" is essentially a huge adult playground, striking a chord across several generations. Millennials grew up with "Grand Theft Auto III," "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City," "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," and "Grand Theft Auto IV," while Gen Z grew up with "Grand Theft Auto V." Generation Alpha might still be too young for the latest edition, but will likely find ways to play it anyway.

blocks.caption: In 'GTA VI,' Lucia and Jason play a gangster couple; the players' actions determine how close they becomeImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Social media has certainly played a part in the series' ongoing success, particularly "GTA V" and its multiplayer spin-off, "GTA Online." Numerous content creators stream gameplay sessions on Twitch or YouTube, and particularly funny or crazy gameplay moments end up on TikTok.

At the same time, a dedicated role-play community has grown around the game. Players gather inside the world of "GTA" to act out specific characters, such as taxi drivers, judges or small-time criminals. They invent realistic backstories for their personas, and many even use accents to stay in character.
Perfectionism has its downsides

The hype surrounding "GTA VI" is not only good news for the game itself but could also boost the entire games industry by drawing more people back to their consoles. This is because the boom triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic was followed by studio closures and redundancies. Worldwide, it's estimated that 50,000 people in the games industry have lost their jobs since 2022.

But while publisher Rockstar Games is well-known for the meticulous polish of its titles and attention to detail, the perfectionism so prized by fans also has its drawbacks, especially for those working on the game. Rockstar, like many other game developers, has frequently faced major criticism regarding its labor practices.

blocks.caption: 'GTA' characters can relax at Leonida Keys, but game developers face high-pressure workloads in the lead-up to game releasesImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Former developers report extremely long working hours and a heavy workload that resulted in health issues. Trade unions accuse company managers of employee surveillance, resulting in a culture of workplace stress and low morale.

Coinciding with the launch of Rockstar's largest game to date, the developers behind it are pushing for trade union recognition. That move would give them a collective voice to address working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. If successful, their campaign could set a major precedent for the wider video game industry, which continues to face challenges around fair labor practices.
This article was originally written in German.
Hooked on video gaming

articles.title: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
articles.summary: Watch: The BBC's Jonathan Beale joins Ukrainian forces who have taken the battle below ground and out of sight of Russian drones.

blocks.text: For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.

With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.
Read Jonathan Beale's dispatch from the front line.

articles.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
articles.summary: Ukrainian forces are fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet tunnel in the Kharkiv region.

blocks.text: Watch: Inside the gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
ByJonathan Beale
Defence correspondent, near Kupyansk
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

blocks.caption: Map showing the location of a gas pipeline in north-eastern Ukraine near Kupyansk. A red line marks the pipeline running from east to west to the north of the Kupyansk. The map indicates that the area in the north east of the map is currently under Russian military control. This area is extended…

blocks.text: Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro

blocks.text: Image source, Moose Campbell/BBC
Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.

They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.

Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.

Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground

blocks.text: Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.

But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.

Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."

His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe

blocks.text: The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.

Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.

Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.

blocks.caption: A Ukrainian soldier call sign Zanuda stands in a black hoodie and black cap in front of a sign reading Khartiya

blocks.text: Moose Campbell/BBC
Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground

blocks.caption: "Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground", Source: Zanuda, Source description: Ukrainian soldier, Image: A Ukrainian soldier call sign Zanuda stands in a black hoodie and black cap in front of a sign reading Khartiya

blocks.text: While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.

But, Zanuda believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."
In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.
It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success. It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale. But on its own it has not changed the course of the war.
For Ukraine, there is still no light at the end of the tunnel.
Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann
